title: The Ardennes Campaign Simulation Data Base (ACSDB)
author: Data Memory Systems, Inc.
organization: Data Memory Systems, Inc., 10392 Democracy Lane, Fairfax, VA 22030
data_description:
a. The Ardennes Campaign Simulation Data Base (ACSDB) is a computerized data base of the World War II campaign fought in December 1944 and January 1945, popularly known as the "Battle of the Bulge." It uses the dBASEIVTM data base management system to facilitate storage and manipulation. The data include daily information on unit location, activities, order of battle, personnel, equipment, and logistics at the army, corps, division, and brigade level for the period 16 December 1944 through 16 January 1944, plus data on tactical air operations, tables of organization and equipment (TO/E) of units, and equipment used by opposing forces in the Ardennes Campaign. The computerized portion of the ACSDB is about 39 megabytes in size. It is supplemented by the written reports containing bibliographic, definitional, and other information; a set of full-scale color photographs of 1/100,000 scale maps of the Ardennes region with a clear acetate overlay on which are shown locations of US and German units on 16 December 1944; a user's guide for the ACSDB; a narrative on the single-shot probability of kill (SSPK) data researched for the ACSDB; and a collection of photocopies of all records used for generation of the ACSDB totaling some 10 cubic feet of printed material.

b. (pg IV-i) "The Unit Location Data Base of the Ardennes Campaign Simulation Data Base (ACSDB) is used to record daily information on the activities and locations of US, British, and German ground units at division-level and above."

c. The source obtained its data from both primary and secondary sources.

- (1) The primary records used for daily information on frontline locations, boundaries between frontline units, and other unit location data included US Army daily SITREPS (Situation Reports) and British Army War Diaries, and OKW briefing maps (which were prepared three times daily using red and blue color markings to show the locations of German and Allied units on topographical maps of the area).
- (2) Other sources included unit histories, official histories, and chronologies. Use was also made of the manuscripts prepared by German division, corps and army commanders as part of the US Army's postwar Foreign Military Studies program.
- (3) Daily unit location data was generated using the same general approach for all three nations. First the daily locations of divisions and brigades were determined. This information was then reviewed and their frontline traces compiled to generate the data on corps. The process was repeated using corps data for armies. Finally, the frontline traces and locations of other significant unit elements of all forces were checked by comparing the daily frontline locations of opposing Allied and German units. This step was necessary because the unit location data of opposing forces was derived separately. The proofing process involved plotting grid coordinates of units using the graphics feature of the ReflexTM data base management software. This check showed remarkably close correlation between the frontline traces of the opposing forces. testimony to the accuracy of the German maps, the Allied situation reports, and the postwar manuscripts of the German officers.

d. The following information is given in the Unit Location Data Base part of the ACSDB (quoted from pp IV-1 to IV-7 of the source).

- (1) Unit Name; Field 1. Identification of the unit for which location data is recorded in the record is provided under "Unit Name." The designations used for divisions and Brigades are the same ones used in the Unit and Unit Inventory Data Bases [which are other parts of the ACSDB]. For corps and armies, only the title of the unit is entered (i.e., "5th PzArmy," "XXX Corps," "1st Army," "III Corps," "I SSPzK," etc.), unlike the entries used in the Unit and Unit Inventory Data Bases which differentiate between corps/army headquarters and corps/army troops ("5th PzArmy Troops," "XXX Corps Troops," "1st Army HQ," etc.).
- (2) Date; Field 2. Provided under "Date" is the date in month-day-year format of the record. See the ACSDB Time Conventions narrative [not reproduced here] for definitions of time periods for the US, British, and German records in the Unit Location Data Base.
- (3) Nationality; Field 3. This is the nationality of the unit for which data is recorded. "A" designates American (US), "B" designates British, and "G" designates German.
- (4) Parent Unit; Field 4. Recorded under "Parent Unit" is the identification of the immediate superior unit of the unit tracked in the Unit Location Record. Designations recorded under "Parent Unit" are the same as those used for "Unit Name," i.e., "5th PzArmy," "I SSpzK," "XXX Corps," "1st Army," etc.
- (5) HQ Starting Location; Field 5. Recorded under "HQ Starting Location" is the location of the unit's headquarters at the beginning of the day. Its location is designated in all cases by the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) four- or six-digit grid coordinates used on the 1943 Geographical Section, General Staff maps produced by the Army Map Service. These maps are:

| Sheet# | Name |
|---|---|
| 8 | Brussels |
| 9 | Liege |
| 12 | Namur |
| 13 | Marche |
| 16 | Mezieres |
| 14 | Arlon |
| R-1 | Koeln |
| S-1 | Bonn |
| T-1 | Trier |
| V-1 | Neunkirchen |

If information is available, an actual place location name is included, most commonly a town, village, or city name.

- (6) Mission; Field 6. This is a text field, i.e., information recorded in this field is in text format. Under "Mission" is recorded a unit's basic mission for the day, including planned activities, operations, changes in organization, and other pertinent information. This is a "required" data field, i.e., information on unit mission is provided in the Unit Location Data Base for each unit for every day.
- (7) Displacement; Field 7. Under "Displacement" is recorded:
- (a) The straight-line distance in kilometers that the center of a unit's frontline moved during the 24 hours beginning at 0600 hours of the date recorded under "Date," or
- (b) The straight-line distance in kilometers that the headquarters of a unit moved during the 24 hours beginning at 0600 hours of the date recorded under "Date," or
- (c) The straight-line distance in kilometers that the center of mass of a unit moved during the 24 hours beginning at 0600 hours of the date recorded under "Date," or
- (d) Any other straight-line movement distance (in kilometers) moved by a unit from one point to another as specified under "Remarks" [cf. Fields 22, 28 and 29].

The "Displacement" value is always positive. Displacement can indicate movement of a unit while in reserve or transit. Case (a) above is always used to describe unit movement while the unit is in a frontline position. The movement can be forward, lateral, or retrograde movement. Cases (b) to (d) depend on the nature and availability of the information found in data sources. When not self-evident in meaning, data recorded under "Displacement" is always explained under "Remarks" [cf. Fields 22, 28, and 29] to facilitate understanding of a unit's movement.

- (8) Distance Opposed Advanced; Field 8. Data recorded under "Distance Opposed Advanced" is the distance in kilometers that a unit moves in combat and is only used to record data when a unit or significant elements of it are in the frontline. "Distance Opposed Advanced" is a subset of location displacement, and its absolute value never exceeds the value of "Displacement." Positive values entered under "Distance Opposed Advanced" represent advances or forward movement, and negative values represent retrograde movement.
- (9) Width of Front; Field 9. Entered under "Width of Front" is a unit's frontline width (in kilometers), bounded on its flanks by the grid coordinates provided under "Left Flank" and "Right Flank" (Fields 10 and 11) and following a frontline trace delineated by grid coordinates provided under "REFERENCE POINTS" (Fields 12-15 and 34-37). When a unit is in transit behind or in reserve out of the frontline, a value of 0.0 is provided under "Width of Front." The front and rear of a unit march column may also be provided under "Left Flank" and "Right Flank." When information in sources is available, the route of a march column is identified by grid coordinates recorded under "REFERENCE POINTS." Data in "REFERENCE POINTS" is also used to describe the outline of a unit's "goose egg" position when it is in reserve. In cases where information in sources on a unit's location in reserve was minimal, only one or two "REFERENCE POINTS" may be used to identify the unit's location.
- (10) Separate Elements; Fields 30-33. Data entered under "Separate Elements" (using grid coordinates) describes the location of major elements of a unit not in the immediate vicinity of the main body of the unit, such as detached organic elements of the unit, or units in transit to the main body of the unit. When necessary, amplification of data recorded under "Separate Elements" is provided under "Remarks" [cf. Fields 22, 28, and 29].
- (11) Total Time in Combat, Total Time Not in Combat, and Ancillary Fields: Fields 16-21. Data entered in Fields 16-21 record the duration and time periods of a unit's participation in combat or its time out of combat. Data is provided in these fields when available in sources.
- (12) Major Decisions/Redirections, Other Significant Events, and Remarks; Fields 22, 28, and 29. These are text fields provided for explanation of a unit's activities and any interpretive remarks to clarify data provided in other fields. Information is provided in these fields when it is available or pertinent to the understanding of data entered in any other field. In practice, due to limitations of text space in the computer data format, the use of the fields is interchangeable, i.e., they are all employed to record any textual information on a unit's activities, location, mission, displacement, etc.
- (13) Unit Commander Data; Field 23. This is a text field. Entered under "Unit Commander Data" are the name and rank of the commander of a unit. When a change in command occurs, it is also recorded under "Unit Commander Data." German commanders' rank titles are used for commanders of German units.
- (14) Fortifications; Field 24. This is a text field. Recorded under "Fortifications" is information on permanent and field fortifications maintained and occupied by a unit or other units of the same nationality, which are located in the vicinity of the unit. Information is provided in this field when available in sources.
- (15) Obstacles; Field 25. This is a text field. Recorded under "Obstacles" is information on permanent and field fortifications of a unit's opponents, or natural obstructions such as woods, rivers, and steep terrain in the vicinity of the unit. Information is provided in this field when available in sources.
- (16) Surface Trafficability; Field 26. This is a text field. Recorded under "Surface Trafficability" is information describing the condition of the ground and roads in the vicinity of the unit. Information is provided in this field when available in sources.
- (17) Weather; Field 27. This is a text field. Recorded under "Weather" is information on climatic conditions for the 24-hour period on the indicated date and in the vicinity of the unit. Information is frequently taken verbatim from sources and is thus recorded in the format or style of the source.
- (18) Sources; (no field number). Each unit has a unique corresponding Reference Data Base record which lists all sources used to compile unit location data for that unit. The Reference Data Base record is identified by a unique alphanumeric code, which is also entered under "Sources" in the Unit Location Data Base records of the corresponding unit. Attachment 1 [not reproduced here] contains a list with the names of units and the alphanumeric codes of their corresponding Reference Data Base records. These are the same codes entered under "Sources" in the Unit Location Data Base records. Note that the specific sources used for each item of information are not provided in the relevant Reference Data Base records. Instead, sources and the page numbers consulted in them are listed as the reference material for "All" data. This format proved necessary because of the impracticability of referencing every piece of data in the Unit Location Data Base, a task which would have resulted in the creation of an excessively large series of reference records for the Unit Location Data Base.

e. (pg X-2) "All location data (headquarters location, frontline trace, location of other significant elements) is as of 0600 hours of the indicated date. All 'dynamic' location data (displacement, distance opposed advanced, activities, and operations) occurs in the 24 hours between 0600 hours of the indicated date and 0559 hours of the immediately subsequent date."
discussion_and_comments:
a. This is a major effort to produce a comprehensive quantitative record of the events that occurred during the Ardennes Campaign. The data are in a form that lends itself to ready retrieval and collation.

b. Since the data were entered by several individuals at many different times, it was not possible to stick exactly to the stated data base format. A few slips were found while extracting the following sample of items from the Unit Location data base file.

c. Also, missing values are variously coded as "99999999," "999.9," or as a blank field with no entries. This must be taken into account when using computer programs to process the data.

d. Fields 6 (Mission), 22 (Major Decisions), 24 (Fortifications), 25 (Obstacles), 26 (Surface Trafficability), 27 (Weather), 28 (Other Significant Events), and 29 (Remarks) are not coded in any standard form. Hence, for example, the same weather conditions may be variously described as "fog," "foggy," "limited visibility," "visibility limited to 100-200 meters," "moderately foggy," "fog obscured enemy positions," "visibility of enemy positions limited," "visibility hampered operations," etc. Computer processing of the information in these fields is inconvenient (to say the least) in their present format. With enough additional work, it might be possible to convert the information to a standard format.

e. There is no direct record in the data base as to which of the distances mentioned in paragraph 2e(7) was actually entered into Fields 7 (Displacement) and 8 (Distance Opposed Advance). To some extent that information can be inferred from the context, but not in a way that is conveniently programmed for computer manipulation of the information.
data_table_notes:
a. The Unit Location file is much too large to be reproduced here. However, an extract of the Unit Location file is given in the accompanying tables. The full ACSDB is available at CAA.

b. As noted in paragraphs 3c and 3d above, some of the data fields are not in a form that lends itself easily to processing by computer programs. The fields that do lend themselves to computer processing are given here.

c. Even so, the data base is so large we had to break it into sections. We used the following time intervals to divide the data into seven sections:

| 2 | 20-24 Dec 44 |
| 3 | 25-29 Dec 44 |
| 4 | 30 Dec 44-3 Jan 45 |
| 5 | 04-08 Jan 45 |

title: Alexander: A History of the Origin and Growth of the Art of War from the Earliest Times to the Battle of the Ipsus, BC 301, With a Detailed Account of the Campaigns of the Great Macedonian
author: Dodge, Theodore Ayrault
organization: The Riverside Press, Cambridge (Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston and New York)
data_description:
a. Appendix A of the source tabulates distances and elapsed times for "Some Ancient Marches." This source table gives distances and times of march for some ancient marches, together with the year in which the march was made and the number and kind of troops participating in it. These are given in the first 19 rows of the data base.

b. Appendix C of the source gives a table of distances for the "Marches of Alexander." These are also given in our ALEXANDE data base.
discussion_and_comments:
a. All these advances apparently were but lightly opposed. The values can be compared to those in the ENGELS data base.

b. This is one of a series of volumes by Theodore Ayrault Dodge. See, for example, the data bases given elsewhere for CAESAR, GUSTAVUS, HANNIBAL, and NAPOLEON.

c. The ALEXANDE data base provides information only on forces that are lightly engaged.

d. Some of the subtotals in Dodge's table of "Marches of Alexander" appear to be in error. These errors very nearly cancel out, so Dodge's grand total is very nearly accurate.
data_table_notes:
a. Note 1: "Some of the distances are taken from Colonel Chesney; some are from Kiepert's maps. Exact accuracy has not been aimed at, as the old roads and the location of many places are not known."

b. For 3 of his 19 notable marches, Dodge stated that the distance was "over" a certain figure. In our data base we indicated this by a "+" following the distance in miles.

title: Rates of Advance in Land Attack Against Unprepared Forces
author: Andrews, Marshall
organization: Operations Research Office, 6935 Arlington Road, Bethesda, MD
data_description:
a. The ANDREWS data are taken from Tables 1 and 2 of the source. Andrews in turn used Esposito, Vincent J. (ed.), "The West Point Atlas of American Wars," 2 vols, Praeger, New York, 1959 as a source of advance distances and durations for all of the cases he investigated.

b. Andrews presents data on the 14 advances listed below. The first three of these advances were made by infantry on foot supported by horse-drawn artillery and screened by horse cavalry. The others were carried out either with substantial armored support or as predominantly armored operations. Andrews' goal was not to derive an absolute number applicable to a specific situation or type of operation, but to obtain an average applicable for planning purposes to any of a number of comparable instances sharing the common characteristic of a massive attack by fully prepared forces against a relatively unprepared opponent. In each case the criterion for distance advanced was attainment of the objective or cessation of the advance due to defensive action, whether by the opponent or by other factors.

List of the Fourteen Campaigns Studied by Andrews

| Case no. | Short name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sherman | Sherman's march from Atlanta to Savannah, Georgia |
| 2 | Kluck | German invasion of Belgium and France, August-September 1914 |
| 3 | Caporetto | Austro-German advance from Caporetto, November 1917 |
| 4 | Kleist | German invasion of Holland, Belgium and France, May 1940 |
| 5 | 4th Army | Advance of the German 4th Army from the Somme, June 1940 |
| 6 | Yugoslavia & Greece | German invasion of Yugoslavia and Greece, April 1941 |
| 7 | Russia | German invasion of Russia, June-December 1941 |
| 8 | Malaya | Japanese advance through Malaya to Singapore, 1941-1942 |
| 9 | North Korea | North Korean invasion of South Korea, June-August 1950 |
| 10 | Wavell | British advance from Sidi Barrani to Beda Fomm, North Africa, December 1940-February 1941 |
| 11 | Rommel I | German advance from El Agheila to Salum, North Africa, March-May 1941 |
| 12 | Auchinleck | British advance from Salum to El Agheila, North Africa, November-December 1941 |
| 13 | Rommel II | German advance from El Agheila to El Alamein, North Africa, January-July 1942 |
| 14 | Montgomery | British advance from El Alamein to the Mareth Line, North Africa, October 1942 to January 1943 |

c. Andrews defines his distances as the distance between the phase lines shown in "The West Point Atlas of American Wars," and explains (pp 8-9) that "These results do not, nor could they, take into consideration actual road miles covered by major or subordinate units. Distances used are in terms of distance covered over stated periods. ...No attempt has been made to include vertical distance in the total miles traveled ... In each case selected the criterion for distances advanced was attainment of the objective or cessation of the advance. It was not considered whether fractions of the command charged with the operation, or the entire force, had closed up on the objective so long as the objective itself was realized. On the other hand, penetrations by small subordinate units, such as reconnaissance elements, beyond the final phase line were disregarded."
discussion_and_comments:
a. As its title indicates, this is a study of rates of advance by forces that are but lightly engaged. I suspect that earlier on, various staff studies may have collected similar data and made some sort of informal or even statistical analysis of it-witness the fairly definite march rate examples Clausewitz put forward (Clausewitz, 1832), but Andrews' study is the first systematic effort that has come to my attention.

b. I have not always been able to reconcile the times quoted by Andrews with the dates he gives. Several of Andrews' advance rates are not accurate to the number of significant figures shown in his tables. For example, Andrews' entry of 3.00 for the rate of advance in Caporetto-Phase 2 is surely a misprint and should read 3.60 miles/day. Some other values are good only to "slide rule accuracy," i.e., to two or three significant figures.

c. We did not attempt to determine whether Andrews' distances and durations accurately represent the maps in the West Point Atlas of American Wars.

d. Andrews gives a third table (his Table 3, entitled *Rates of Advance in Mountain Terrain*), but it merely duplicates the entries for Yugoslavia, Greece, and North Korea in his Table 1.
data_table_notes:
a. Andrews does not give information on the intensity of opposition, the topography, vegetation, or footing. I have supplied the values shown for these items, but they are little better than guesses on my part and should not be taken too seriously unless confirmed by more authoritative sources. This is an exception to the general rule that I do not supply information not actually given by the source.

b. The entries in the data base column headed "Notes" gives the specific table in the source from which the entry was taken.

title: An Analysis of Infantry Rates of Advance in Battle
author: Gould, A. H., and H. Gee
organization: British Army Operational Research Group, Department of the Scientific Adviser to the Army Council
available_from: Defense Operational Analysis Establishment, United Kingdom
data_description:
a. The source gives the advance distances and times of 331 small unit infantry engagements in World War II. Of these, 164 are from Italy during the months of January, June, July and October 1944; the remaining 167 are from Northwest Europe during the months of January to March 1945. They were gathered to determine the feasibility of quoting a figure representative of "the average rate of infantry advance," at the same time assessing the influence of a number of operational variables on (a) the rate of advance and (b) the associated casualties per company.

b. The units involved ranged in size from one to four companies of infantry supported by various levels of artillery, tanks and other armored vehicles, and air as part of a combined arms operation. They are distributed as follows:

| No. of infantry cos. involved | No. of actions |
|---|---|
| 1 | 56 |
| 2 | 74 |
| 3 | 194 |
| 4 | 7 |
| Total | 331 |

c. The following data are given:

- (1) "Strength of our own troops in terms of numbers of companies in attack."
- (2) "Distance in yards covered by infantry on foot in the advance from start line to objective."
- (3) "Time taken from crossing the start line to the leading troops reaching the objective."
- (4) "Type of country typified by the Theatres of War, i.e., Northwest Europe or Italy, these being representative of relatively flat and mountainous going respectively." The source also indicates the general area involved (e.g., Holland, Reichwald Area, Cleve, etc.).
- (5) "Within each area [i.e., Theatre of War], [type of terrain] by the local nature of the country, defined as open, close (i.e., wooded) or built-up."
- (6) "Advance by day or night."
- (7) "Number of casualties suffered by own troops."
- (8) "Although in many actions some statement of the fire support was made, in general the description lacked precision, such statements as "RA" or "Tanks" being the sole description. It was considered impractical to give measure to such general statements and consequently this factor has not been incorporated into the analysis." However, the source notes when such statements were given in the War Diaries.
- (9) "Similarly the strength of enemy opposition has been classified under only two headings, heavy and slight, again without allowance being made for the variations within these headings. No detail was available as to the support arms used by the enemy."

d. The source notes that it was not considered feasible to obtain usable information on such factors as:

- (1) Influence of prearranged plan.
- (2) Weather conditions prevailing at the time of the action.
- (3) Training and battle experience of the troops.
- (4) Amount and duration of fire support.
- (5) Extent and value of previous reconnaissance.
- (6) The source also notes that "No detail was available as to the support arms used by the enemy."
discussion_and_comments:
a. This is an excellent study, clearly and concisely reported. The data seem to be exceptionally carefully compiled. BAORG has a high reputation in the military operational analysis community for the accuracy and conscientiousness of their wartime data collection work. This appears to be the earliest study that attempts in a systematic way to assess quantitatively the influence of various factors upon rates of advance in land combat, or to employ modern statistical techniques to analyze the data.

b. (p 3) "It was not possible, of course, to estimate to what degree the rates of advance which were studied were conditioned by previous planning. This element would be particularly important in timed operations employing two or three companies."

c. (p 3) "Whilst it is reasonable to assume that [the prevailing weather conditions] may materially affect the course of the action, this factor had to be neglected as, in the majority of instances, no precise statement of weather conditions was available."

d. (p 3) "[Training and battle experience of the troops], which applies not only to our forces but also to the enemy forces opposing the advance, is again neglected for reasons similar to those stated above in respect of [weather conditions]."

e. (p 3) "(Extent and value of previous reconnaissance) is again neglected for the reasons applicable to [weather and training]."

f. The extent to which the War Diary entries suffered from a potential vicious circle is not known. The vicious circle referred to here is the one that bases judgmental assessments of such factors as enemy opposition and closeness of the terrain at least in part upon the rate of advance achieved. That is, it is easy to slip inadvertently into judging enemy resistance as slight because the rate of advance was high, and then to turn around and argue that the rate of advance was high because enemy opposition was slight. This sort of vicious circle can be broken only if the assessments of enemy resistance and rate of advance are completely independent of one another. Without detailed knowledge of the particulars of the case, it is hard to say whether these assessments were dependent or independent.

g. On the basis of inspection of the advance distance tables, it appears that there is a significant bias in the direction of reporting attacks that gained ground as opposed to those that did not.

h. All of the values given in the source were taken from War Diaries "as accurately as the records permitted, but the degree of accuracy of these figures is not known." Also, the distances from the start line to the objective were in general derived from map square references and so do not necessarily represent a true figure of the actual distance which may have been traveled.

i. The BAORG data deal with forces that are heavily engaged. The differentiation between heavy and slight enemy opposition must be interpreted as differing degrees of opposition within that context.
data_table_notes: While mode of transportation is listed as "foot," note frequent substantial tank support and organization as combined arms teams.

title: Caesar-A History of the Art of War Among the Romans Down to the End of the Roman Empire, With a Detailed Account of the Campaigns of Caius Julius Caesar
author: Dodge, Theodore Ayrault
organization: The Riverside Press, Cambridge, Houghton, Mifflin, and Co, Boston and New York
data_description: The CAESAR data are taken from the table entitled "Some Ancient Marches" of the source's Appendix B. This table gives distances and times of march for some ancient marches, together with the year in which the march was made and the number and kind of troops participating in it.
discussion_and_comments:
a. All of the marches recorded in the source took place between 490 BC and 46 BC. Most of them are for Greeks (19 out of 27 marches) and partly duplicate those in the ALEXANDE data base. They are for forces that are only lightly engaged.

b. The author has a sound reputation as a military historian and apparently took some care to make these data as accurate as he could. However, in statistical terms they are a "convenience sample," and not necessarily a random one.

c. For some other works by Dodge, see data bases ALEXANDE, CAESAR, GUSTAVUS, HANNIBAL, and NAPOLEON.
data_table_notes:
a. Some of the values in the original table are estimates (the "+" indicates that the estimate is believed to be an underestimate).

b. The one Note reads "Desert. The end of thirty-six hours continuous marching; of eleven days of nearly forty miles a day."

title: CAA's Combat Data Base-Version 1990 (CDB90)
author: Helmbold, Robert L.
organization: US Army Concepts Analysis Agency
data_description: CDB90 is based on information collected over a period of several years by the Historical Evaluation and Research Organization and recently acquired and revised under CAA's supervision. It contains tabulated data on 660 battles and engagements that occurred between 1600 and 1973. About 90 items of information are given on each battle in the data base. In most cases, this includes the elapsed time for the battle and the distance advanced (or withdrawn) by the attacker. However, the rate of advance for some battles cannot be found from the information in the data base.
discussion_and_comments:
a. Fragments or earlier versions of this data base have appeared. The current version includes and supersedes all earlier versions. Without attempting to be exhaustive, we note that fragments or earlier versions of this data base appeared in or were used by the following:

- (1) McQuie, Robert, et al, "Multivariate Analysis of Combat," PRC R-1143, Planning Research Corporation, July 1968.
- (2) Warner, C. A., "An Examination of Rates of Advance as a Function of Force Ratios for Ground Combat War Games," published as Appendix G of Methods of Force Requirements Determination (MEFORD), RAC-R-121, Research Analysis Corporation, 1970, McLean, VA, AD-515 716L.
- (3) "Use of Historical Data in Evaluating Military Effectiveness," Historical Evaluation and Research Organization, 1970.
- (4) "A Study of the Relationship of Tactical Air Support Operations to Land Combat," Historical Research and Evaluation Organization, 1971.
- (5) Pearsall, Edward S., "Casualty Rates and Opposed Advance," Working Paper No. 11, Institute for Defense Analyses, January 1972 (also presented to the Improved Methodologies for General Purposes Planning: New Methods Study).
- (6) "FEBA Movement and Attrition Processes," War Gaming Directorate, CAA-SP-75-1, US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, 21 February 1975.
- (7) Dupuy, Trevor N., "Numbers, Predictions and War: Using History to Evaluate Combat Factors and Predict the Outcome of Battles," The Bobbs-Merrill Company, Indianapolis, IN, 1979. (Slightly different versions of CDB-90 have also been used as part of the factual basis for Dupuy's Quantified Judgment Method, abbreviated as QJM.)
- (8) "Integrated Warfare-Representing the Decision Process Within Computer Simulations of Combat," CAA-TP-85-1, US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, January 1985.
- (9) Helmbold, Robert L., "Combat History Analysis Study Effort (CHASE): A Progress Report for the Period August 1984-June 1985," CAA-TP-86-2, US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, August 1986, AD-F860 122.
- (10) Dupuy, Trevor N., "Can We Rely Upon Computer Combat Simulations?," Armed Forces Journal International, August 1987, pp 58-63.
- (11) Helmbold, Robert L., "Do Battles and Wars Have a Common Relationship Between Casualties and Victory?," CAA-TP-87-16, US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, November 1987.
- (12) McQuie, Robert, "Historical Characteristics of Combat for Wargames (Benchmarks)," Research Paper CAA-RP-87-2, US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, July 1988, AD-200 036.
- (13) "Forced Changes in Combat Posture," unnumbered DMSI report, 30 September 1988, prepared for CAA by Data Memory Systems, Inc. under Contract No. MDA903-87-C-0807, AD-A201 405.
- (14) "New Engagement Data for the Breakpoint Data Base," unnumbered DMSI report, 30 September 1988, prepared for CAA by Data Memory Systems, Inc. under Contract No. MDA903-87-C-0807, AD-A201 404.
- (15) "Description of the Combat Data Base-Version 1990 (CDB-90)," US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, to be published.

b. Much effort has gone into developing and improving this data base, because (as evidenced by the works cited above) it has applications in many areas. The major recent efforts began with "Analysis of Factors That Have Influenced Outcomes of Battles and Wars: A Data Base of Battles and Engagements," US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, Study Report CAA-SR-84-6, in six volumes, September 1984, prepared for CAA by the Historical Evaluation and Research Organization (HERO) under Contract Number MDA903-82-C-0363, available from the Defense Technical Information Center (DTIC) as follows:

| Volume no. | AD Number |
|---|---|
| 1 | B-086 797L |
| 2 | B-087 718L |
| 3 | B-087 719L |
| 4 | B-087 720L |
| 5 | B-087 721L |
| 6 | B-087 722L |

It was recognized that corrections, clarifications, and expansions, of this version of the data base were needed. Many of these were addressed in "CHASE Data Enhancement Study (CDES)," Historical Evaluation and Research Organization (HERO), Report Number 129, in five volumes, 31 January 1986. Prepared for US Army Concepts Analysis Agency (CAA) under Contract Number MDA903-85-C-0252, and available from DTIC as AD-A175 712, AD-A175 713, AD-A175 714, AD-A175 715, and AD-A175 716. Some of the remaining errors were corrected in "Data Base Error Correction (DBEC)," unnumbered HERO report, 23 January 1987, prepared for CAA under Purchase Order Number MDA903-86-M-8560, AD-A176 750. A parallel independent review and evaluation of some data that appeared to be statistically anomalous was described in "Independent Review/ Reassessment of Anomalous Data (IR/RAD)," unnumbered LFW Management Associates, Inc. Report, 22 June 1987, in four volumes, prepared for CAA under Contract Number MDA903-86-C-0396, and available from DTIC as AD-195 381 (Volume I), AD-195 726 (Volume II), AD-195 382 (Volume III), and AD-195 383 (Volume IV). However, the present version (CDB-90) does not use the changes suggested by the IR/RAD work.

c. Despite the efforts made to refine this data base, some problems may remain.

- (1) First, there is the matter of anomalous data which was first raised in the CHASE progress report mentioned above and largely confirmed by the IR/RAD report and by Helmbold, Robert L. "Do Battles and Wars Have a Common Relationship Between Casualties and Victory?," CAA-TP-87-16, US Army Concepts Analysis Agency, November 1987. This anomaly clouds the relation between casualties and victory in battle. Whether it also obscures the relation between casualties and rates of advance remains to be seen.
- (2) Second, there is a potential for attacker bias in the rates of advance. The first version of this data (CAA Study Report CAA-SR-84-6, in six volumes, September 1984, cited above) defined the distance advanced to be "The distance, in kilometers, from the line of departure to the farthest point reached by significant maneuver elements of the attacking force, measured along the axis of advance (emphasis added)." Logically then, the recorded distance advanced could never be negative, since no values would be reported for occasions on which the attacker was thrown back. For instance, a net attacker loss of 3 km after a brief penetration of 2 km would be recorded the same way as (and look exactly like) a 2 km gain made and held at the end of the battle. That there was such an attacker bias in the original version is confirmed by the fact that out of 601 battles, only a handful of negative advance distances were recorded. Later efforts to correct this attacker bias (described in the documents cited in paragraph b above) appear to have been only partly successful. Hence, there is a suspicion that a substantial attacker bias still remains in CDB90.
- (3) Third, the actions for sequence numbers 602 through 660, which were added later, have many missing values and do not appear to be of the same quality as the others with regard to accuracy and validity.

d. The CDB90 data base gives data on forces that are heavily engaged.
data_table_notes:
a. The CDB90 data tables are too extensive to give in full here. The reader is advised to consult the work cited in paragraph 3a(15), above, for the complete CDB-90 data base.

b. The fragment of the CDB90 data base given here includes those portions specifically related to distances, durations, and rates of advance. The coding scheme is explained in the following paragraphs.

c. SEQNO is an arbitrary index or sequence number.

d. NAME is the name of the battle.

e. DATE is the date the battle started, given as the year and fraction thereof.

f. WOFA1 is the attacker's width of front at the start of the battle, in km. WOFD1 is the corresponding item for the defender.

g. POST1 is the defender's primary defensive posture at the start of the battle, coded as follows: 2 = Fortified defense, 1 = Prepared defense, 0 = Hasty defense, -1 = Delaying action adopted, -2 = Withdrawal adopted, -9 = Not reported in the source.

h. TERRA1 is terrain code 1, coded as follows: 2 = Rugged, 1 = Rolling, 0 = Flat, -9 = Not reported in the source.

i. TERRA2 is terrain code 2, coded as follows: 2 = Wooded, 1 = Mixed, 0 = Bare, -1 = Desert, -9 = Not reported in the source.

j. TERRA3 is terrain code 3, coded as follows: 2 = Urban, 1 = Marsh or swamp, 0 = Dunes, -9 = Not reported in the source.

k. WX1 is weather code 1, coded as follows: 1 = Wet, 0 = Dry, -9 = Not reported in the source.

l. WX2 is weather code 2, coded as follows: 3 = Heavy (precipitation), 2 = Light, 1 = Overcast (no precipitation), 0 = Sunny, -9 = Not reported in the source.

m. WX3 is weather code 3, coded as follows: 1 = Hot, 0 = Mild, 2 = Cold, -9 = Not reported in the source.

n. WX4 is weather code 4, coded as follows: 3 = Fall (season of year), 2 = Summer, 1 = Spring, 0 = Winter, -9 = Not reported in the source.

o. WX5 is weather code 5, coded as follows: 2 = Equatorial (climate), 1 = Desert, 0 = Temperate, -9 = Not reported in the source.

p. SURPA is the relative surprise achieved by the attacker over the defender, coded as follows: 3 = Complete surprise achieved by the attacker, 2 = Substantial surprise achieved by the attacker, 1 = Minor surprise achieved by the attacker, 0 = Neither side achieved surprise, or it did not affect the outcome, -1 = Minor surprise achieved by the defender, -2 = Substantial surprise achieved by the defender, -3 = Complete surprise achieved by the defender, -9 = Not reported in the source.

q. AEROA is the attacker's relative general air superiority in the theater, coded as follows: 1 = Attacker had air superiority in the theater, 0 = Neither side had air superiority, -1 = Defender had air superiority in the theater, -9 = Not reported in the source.

r. STRA is the attacker's total personnel strength committed to the battle. STRD is the corresponding item for the defender.

s. CODEA is the attacker's personnel strength code, coded as follows: 3 = Total strength is the sum of the initial strength and all replacements/reinforcements received over the course of the battle, 2 = Total strength is an average daily strength over the course of the battle, 1 = Total strength is in fact the initial strength, 0 = Not reported in the source. CODED is the corresponding item for the defender.

t. INTSTA is the attacker's initial personnel strength (-1 if unknown). INTSTD is the corresponding item for the defender.

u. RERPA is the attacker's personnel reinforcements/replacements received over the course of the battle (-1 if unknown). RERPD is the corresponding item for the defender.

v. CASA is the attacker's personnel battle casualties (KIA, WIA, MIA, and POW) over the course of the battle (-1 if unknown). CASD is the corresponding item for the defender.

w. FINSTA is the attacker's final personnel strength at the end of the battle (-1 if unknown). FINSTD is the corresponding item for the defender.

x. KMDA is the distance to which the attacker advanced beyond the defender's initial frontline (negative if the attacker is thrown back), in km. If unknown, it is coded as -9999.

y. ACHA is the adjudged attacker's mission achievement score on a scale of 1 (low) to 10 (high), or 0 if not given in the source. ACHD is the corresponding item for the defender.

z. WINA is the side that won the battle, coded as follows: 1 = Attacker won, 0 = Battle was a draw, -1 = Defender won.

aa. CRIT is the criterion on which WINA is assessed, coded as follows: 1 = Which side won is clear-cut, 2 = Win awarded to the side that on balance best achieved its objectives, 0 = Not given in the source.

ab. PRIA1 is the attacker's primary tactical scheme, coded as follows: 5 = River crossing, 4 = Penetration, 3 = Frontal attack, 2 = Double envelopment, 1 = Single envelopment, 0 = Feint, demonstration, or holding attack, -1 = Defensive plan, -2 = Defensive/offensive plan, -9 = Not reported in the source. PRID1 is the corresponding item for the defender.

ac. BATDURN is the duration of the battle from the beginning of its first active period to the end of its last active period, in days.

ad. SUMATP is the sum of the durations of the individual active periods over the course of the battle, in days.

ae. ATPCODE is coded as 1 if the actual time of day at which the active time periods began and ended are given in the source, 0 otherwise. (Unless the actual times of day at which the active periods began and ended are recorded, the values of SUMATP and of BATDURN will be inaccurate. In fact, they will be larger than the corresponding true values. Rates based on inflated SUMATP or BATDURN times will, of course, be biased downward from their true values.)

title: Manual War Gaming: An Historical Analysis of Combat Ratio Versus Rate of Advance
author: de Santis, MAJ Edward
organization: Treatise Submitted to the Faculty of the United States Army Command and General Staff College, 1972
available_from: US Army Command and General Staff College Library
data_description:
a. (p ii, Abstract) "This investigation was conducted to establish a correlation between combat ratio and rates of advance of two opposing forces on a conventional battlefield. The primary purpose of the research was to verify the data presently being used in the Combat Developments Command Manual Quick War Game (JIFFY)."

b. The source provides data on advances in 84 World War II division operations in the European Theater of Operations. It obtained its data from the US Army in WWII Series (Green Books), supplemented by a few other history books.

c. Distances are defined as (p 21) "The actual distance of advance of the attacker in each battle analyzed was scaled off the situation map for the corresponding time interval described in the narrative of the battle."

d. Situational descriptors are defined as follows.

- (1) Type of Attack. (p 18) Frontal or flank attack by infantry or by mechanized/armored attacks over open, median and close terrain.
- (2) Open, Median, or Close terrain (see the Data Table Notes, below).
- (3) Open, Hasty, or Fortified Defense (see the Data Table Notes, below).
discussion_and_comments:
a. The DESANTIS data on rates of advance are highly correlated (i.e., partly redundant), since they are for advances by several of the divisions in a single corps operation. It is doubtful that they should be treated as though they were separate (statistically independent) sample points. Also, some of De Santis' categories contain very few data points, as illustrated below:

| Category | Data points |
|---|---|
| Infantry attacks over open terrain | 25 |
| Mechanized attacks over open terrain | 11 |
| Infantry attacks over close terrain | 10 |
| Infantry attacks over median terrain | 17 |
| Mechanized attacks over median terrain | 15 |
| Mechanized attacks over close terrain | 6 |
| Total | 74 |

b. Most of the data used in this study are for US versus German forces in the European Theater of Operations, nearly all in the October to mid-December 1944 time period. This is a very narrow basis for generalization.

c. These data apply to forces that are heavily engaged.
data_table_notes:
a. Note 1: See source document for definition and procedures for computing firepower ratios.

b. Note 2: (p 17) "Open terrain is flat or slightly rolling, with little vegetation, and has a contour interval variation from 0 to 100 meters per kilometer, permitting maximum cross-country movement. ... Median terrain is rolling terrain, lightly covered with trees and other vegetation with a contour interval variation of 100 to 200 meters per kilometer produced by small hills with gentle slopes causing a slight reduction of cross-country movement.... Close terrain is rough, heavily wooded terrain with a contour interval variation of 200 to 400 meters per kilometer or more. This variation is considered sufficient to cause significant slowing of cross-country movement."

c. Note 3: (pp 16/17). "An open defensive posture is one in which the defender has not had time to prepare field fortifications of any type and is using only the natural cover and concealment afforded by the terrain. ... A hasty defensive posture is one in which basic field fortifications, obstacles, and minefields have been constructed, normally in less than a 24-hour time period. ... A fortified defensive posture is one in which basic field fortifications have been improved with revetments, overhead cover, additional minefields and other obstacles, and the time of preparation of the position has been in excess of 24 hours."

title: Great Battles on the Eastern Front: The Soviet-German War, 1941-1945
author: Dupuy, Trevor N. and Paul Martell
organization: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, Indianapolis
data_description:
a. The EASTFRON data are taken from the tables on pages 45, 58, 89, 128, 148, 163, 182, 191, 203, 217, and 246 of the source.

b. The source states that its information is (p 5) "based primarily on materials in various issues of the Soviet monthly magazine *Military-Historical Journal*". But it is hard to tell exactly what the qualifier "primarily" signifies. For example, although the source briefly alludes (p 2) to some German strength and loss data "taken by the Soviet authors from the German records captured by either by the Red Army or by US forces, the latter available on microfilm at the US National Archives," no other references, bibliographies, or literature citations are offered. None of the source's data are attributed to any *other* source. The source also states (pp 1-2, *passim*) that since "Soviet archives are closed to Western researchers," "it takes an enormous effort to collect Soviet data from the various and numerous sources in Russian open literature and to glean hard data from the propaganda and the unidentified estimates that typically accompany it."

c. Most of the source's data tables provide the distance advanced by a unit and its starting and ending dates. They do not provide explicit information on the intensity of the engagement or the governing mode of movement, topography, vegetation, or footing. Force sizes are implicit in the unit designation. Occasionally orders of battle and unit strengths are given elsewhere in the source. Where a range of values is given for the distances or rates of advance-as in the tables on pages 89 (Kursk), 148 (Crimean Operation), 182 (Lvov-Sandomierz), 203 (East Prussia), 217 (Vistula-Oder), and 246 (Manchuria)-we adopted a "middling" or nominal value computed as the average of the high and low ends of the range given.

d. The EASTFRON data base includes a total of 212 values for the rates of advance gleaned from the following operations: Defense of Moscow, Soviet Counteroffensive, Citadel (Kursk), Melitopol Breakthrough, Melitopol Pursuit, Crimean Operation, Byelorussian Offensive, Lvov-Sandomierz Offensive, Yassy-Kishinev Operation, Battle for East Prussia, Vistula-Oder Offensive, and the Manchurian Campaign.
discussion_and_comments:
a. The data do not include any cases of Soviet retreats or withdrawals-only successful Soviet advances are reported.

b. Some portions of these data can be compared to data on Soviet advances given elsewhere. See, for example, portions of the data bases CDB90, GLANTZ, ORALFORE, RADZIEV, RECORD, SAVKIN, and ROWLAND. See also HERO Combat Data Subscription Service (Volume I, No. 1, 1975; Volume II, No. 1, Winter 1976; Volume II, No. 3, 1977; and Volume II, No. 4, 1978). See also Losik, O. A. (ed.), "Organization and Tactical Employment of Soviet Tank Forces During the Great Patriotic War," Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defense, USSR, Moscow, 1979.

b. These advances are by forces that are lightly engaged. The values given here can be compared with those in, e.g., the ALEXANDE data base.

title: Deep Attack: The Soviet Conduct of Operational Maneuver
author: Glantz, COL David M.
organization: Soviet Army Studies Office, US Army Combined Arms Center, Fort Leavenworth, KS 66027
data_description:
a. The source's goal is to present and to analyze Soviet experiences with operational maneuver. The GLANTZ data are taken from the source's Appendix 4, "Tank Army Operations" and Appendix 5, "Tank/Mechanized Corps Operations."

b. The source does not contain information on the environmental or operational factors such as terrain, weather, vegetation, intensity of opposition, etc.
discussion_and_comments:
a. For the distances, I have used the last two columns of the source's tabulations. Where the source gives two values, I have assumed that they are cumulative and inclusive, and represent the distances from the line or position of commitment to the position reached by the OMG (Operational Maneuver Group) by the end of the corresponding time period (per personal communication from COL Glantz). These are not necessarily the values given by the Soviets. They are the values adopted by COL Glantz on the basis of his research and comparison of Soviet with German maps and archival records. Where cumulative values are given the GLANTZ data base lists their differences, which are the non-cumulative and non-inclusive values.

b. For the times, I have used the last two columns of the source's tabulations. Where the source gives two values, I have assumed that they are cumulative and inclusive (per personal communication from COL Glantz). In such cases the GLANTZ data base lists their differences, which are the non-cumulative and non-inclusive values.

c. The rates given in the GLANTZ data base are simply these distances divided by the corresponding times.

d. The values given for "Day Committed," "Start Date-1," and "End Date-2" are those given by the source.

e. The values given for "Opp'n Intens" are my own rough and doubtless controversial characterization of the intensity of the defender's opposition to the advance. Similarly, the data base values for "Mode of Movement" are my own rough characterization of the predominant or governing mode of movement-the one that dominated the pace of the advance.

f. Some portions of these data can be compared to data on Soviet advances given elsewhere. See, for example, portions of the data bases CDB90, EASTFRON, ORALFORE, RADZIEV, RECORD, SAVKIN, and ROWLAND. See also HERO Combat Data Subscription Service (Volume I, No. 1, 1975; Volume II, No. 1, Winter 1976; Volume II, No. 3, 1977; and Volume II, No. 4, 1978). See also Losik, O. A. (ed.), "Organization and Tactical Employment of Soviet Tank Forces During the Great Patriotic War," Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defense, USSR, Moscow, 1979.

title: Movement
author: Hulse, COL Allen D.
organization: Combat Operations Research Group
available_from: Wainstein, Leonard, "An Examination of the Parsons and Hulse Papers on Rates of Advance," Paper P-991, Institute for Defense Analyses, December 1973, AD-779 848
data_description:
a. The source's purpose was to examine historical data and review the actions played in the CODEM war game in order to improve the modeling of movement.

b. It presents 19 examples from WWII advances made by US armored divisions or mixed task forces within those divisions (chiefly armored battalions or combat commands). Of these, 11 were from NW Europe in 1944, 5 from NW Europe in 1945, and 3 from Italy in 1944.

c. The HULSE data are taken from the source's Enclosure 1. It appears to have obtained its information from after-action reports of the US 1st, 2d, 3d, 4th, and 5th Armored Divisions, and "The US Army in World War II, European Theater of Operations: The Lorraine Campaign" for information on the operations of the US 4th, 6th, and 10th Armored Divisions.

d. Distance is not specifically defined, but presumably is the displacement of the FEBA.

e. The situational descriptors are defined as follows:

- (1) Terrain: Characterized as moderately open, close, mountainous but no objective definitions of these are given.
- (2) Weather: Clear, mild, cold, snow, fog, rain, misty, fair—again objective definitions are not given.
- (3) Type action: Pursuit, limited objective attack, exploitation of a breakthrough, seizure of a deep objective after breaking out of a bridgehead, attack through infantry to seize a deep objective.
- (4) Enemy strength: Very light resistance, heavy, moderate—again without objective definitions.
- (5) Friendly casualties: (seldom known).
- (6) Enemy casualties: (unknown in all cases).
discussion_and_comments:
a. The HULSE data base contains both instances of heavily engaged forces and of lightly engaged forces. The data base itself provides little information on how to distinguish them.

b. The HULSE data base concentrates on armored battalion and combat command operations. See the PARSONS data base for a parallel study of infantry battalion operations.

c. This is a preliminary quick study to find what can be done in the way of collecting and summarizing combat data for use in wargames and analyses. Wainstein (see paragraph 1f, above) has also remarked on that fact and has given a detailed critique of both Hulse's and Parsons' papers. Wainstein observes correctly that:

- (1) Both Hulse's and Parsons' papers are rough, hasty, and tentative reports of initial efforts, rather than finished products intended to provide a firm foundation for broadly-based generalizations.
- (2) Neither Hulse's nor Parsons' numerical data on enemy strength and opposing forces can be historically confirmed.
- (3) Not all of Hulse's and Parsons' distance and duration values can be confirmed by consulting their original sources. Sometimes the original data did not appear to support any specific distance or duration estimate, and in some cases Wainstein found values that differed somewhat from those given by Hulse and Parsons.

title: The Long March, 1935: The Epic of Chinese Communism's Survival
author: Wilson, Dick
organization: Penguin Books, New York, NY (originally published by Hamish Hamilton, LTD, London, 1971)
data_description:
a. The LONGMARX data are taken from "The Daily Itinerary of the Long March," given in Appendix B of the source. It cites the following as its basis:

- (1) Yu Ku, "The Itinerary of the Long March of the Red Army," I-Ching, Shanghai, 20 July 1937, pp 40-44.
- (2) Chu, Li Fu, "Erh-wan Wu-chien Li Chang-cheng Chi (The Long March)," Shanghai, 1937, pp 54-63.

b. The data are for the 1st Army Corps only, and not the main body, which was the 1st Front Army. The 1st Army Corps was the vanguard of the march and covered more distance because of the feints, probes, reconnaissance, and other actions for which it was responsible. The source gives daily advance rates in miles, which it calculated from its sources by taking 3 li to the mile and rounding off fractions.

c. Breaking out of the encirclement of their Kiangsi base by Chiang Kai-Shek's Kuomintang forces on 16 October 1935, about 100,000 Chinese Communists began their Long March (85,000 troops, 15,000 support and administrative personnel, and 35 women). They ended their Long March in Shangsi Province in northwest China on 21 October 1936 with about 8,000 Chinese Communists. They marched on foot, supported by pack animals. Only a handful of the highest ranking commanders rode horses, and no mechanically powered vehicles of any type were used. On the march, the Communists were persistently pursued, harassed, and bombed by Kuomintang forces. Their attrition was due partly to killed; to wounded left behind; to accidents, disease, exposure, starvation, and physical exhaustion; to prisoners, missing and deserters; and to the deliberate formation of small stay-behind groups tasked with gathering intelligence, conducting sabotage and terror operations, starting new revolutionary cells, building local Communist guerilla forces, and politically indoctrinating the populace. The official record of this year-long march claims that the 1st Front Army was involved in an average of one skirmish each day of the march, fought 15 days of major pitched battles, and made 253 marches and 18 night marches, with 100 days of bivouac. One of their commanders stated that they marched over 18 mountain ranges, 5 of which were permanently snow-covered, crossed 24 rivers, took 62 cities or towns, and fought free of at least 10 attempted encirclements by provincial warlords.
discussion_and_comments:
a. The accuracy of the Long March data is questionable. There has been a persistent Chinese Communist tendency to mythologize and propagandize what was, without the need for any exaggeration, one of the most remarkable epics of human struggle and endurance. For example, the Chinese refer to it as "The 25,000-Li March," even though the daily distances in the itinerary sum only to about 18,000 li. Also, while the Mandarin li of about 1/3 miles is the one most commonly used, there are several other distance units used in China, all of different lengths, and all called "li."

b. When the daily distances listed in the source are converted from miles back to li at the rate of 3 li to the mile, with due regard for the rounding off of distances to the nearest mile, it can be seen that the original data must have given daily distances in round numbers of li, normally to the nearest 10 li, and only on a few occasions to the nearest 5 li. Apparently, many of the distances are subjective impressions, or based on recollection, rather than actually measured. According to the source, many of their records were lost to accidents or enemy action during the march, and some of the others were deliberately destroyed to lighten the burden or to prevent their falling into enemy hands.

c. Moreover, 18,000 li travelled in 371 days averages out to 26.0 km/day (16.2 miles/day), including halts and bivouacs—or to 35.6 km/day (22.1 miles/day) if only the 271 marching days are used. These rates of advance are incredibly high for sustained foot marches.

d. The source provides a few schematic maps showing the paths taken by the main elements of the 1st Army Corps on the Long March. Dr. Robert L. Helmbold of CAA has measured the longest and most circuitous of these routes with a map measuring instrument. Five independent measurements were made, and these were averaged to find a total distance travelled of 3,370 miles with a measurement error (standard deviation) of about 50 miles, or 1.5 percent. This is to be compared with the claimed, and oft-quoted, distance of 6,000 miles. The measured distances correspond to only about 10,000 li instead of the 18,000 claimed—much less the poetic 25,000 li. At 3,370 miles, we compute an average of 14.6 km/day (9.1 miles/day) for the elapsed time of 371 days, or 20.0 km/day (12.4 miles/day) for the 271 marching days. These rates of advance, while still rather high and providing evidence of a remarkable feat, are far more credible than the higher figures.

e. The route of the First Front Army is shown on Plate No. 19 of Griess, Thomas E. (ed.), "The West Point Military History Series: Atlas for the Arab-Israeli Wars, the Chinese Civil War, and the Korean War," Avery Publishing Group Inc., Wayne, NJ, 1986. Four measurements of the distance gave an average of 3,265 miles, again with a measurement error (standard deviation) of about 50 miles.

f. Thus, the accuracy and validity of the Long March data seem highly suspect, considering the loss of records, distances reported only to the nearest 10 li, the well-known Chinese tendency to mythologize the Long March, the incredibly high rates of march implied by the longer distance claims, and the disparity between the claimed distances and those measured from the maps.
data_table_notes: The data base gives daily advance distances on the Long March, according to the source. The first day of the march is 16 October 1934, and the 1st Army Corps is recorded as having travelled 10 miles on this day. A question mark (?) is entered when the source gives no distance for some day.
