title: Napoleon—A History of the Art of War, From Lutzen to Waterloo, With a Detailed Account of the Napoleonic Wars
author: Dodge, Theodore Ayrault
organization: AMS Press, New York, NY (for reprint)
data_description:
a. The NAPOLEON data are taken from the table entitled "Some Noteworthy Marches" of Appendix D in Volume 4 of the source.

b. The source table gives distances and times of march for some ancient marches, with some accompanying notes and remarks.
discussion_and_comments:
a. All of the marches recorded in the source took place between 1759 AD and 1815 AD. Most of them are for French troops. The author has a sound reputation as a military historian, and apparently took some care to make these data as accurate as he could. However, in statistical terms they are a "convenience sample," and not necessarily a random one. In any event, they apparently are advances by forces that are unopposed or but lightly engaged.

b. Dodge gives the following tabulation of "average day's marches of an army corps," which he attributes to Colonel Lewal, French staff:

| In | Of | The longest was | The shortest was | The average was |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1796 | 203 marches | 33.5 miles | 5 miles | 15.5 miles |
| 1800 | 135 " | 23.6 " | 2.3 " | 10.6 " |
| 1805 | 267 " | 29.8 " | 7.4 " | 16.1 " |
| 1806 | 94 " | 30.4 " | 3 " | 15.5 " |
| 1815 | 20 " | 19.8 " | 6.2 " | 13.7 " |

Note given in the source, but readily computed from the information above, we find the weighted average rate of march to be 14.75 miles per day, or 23.74 km/day.
data_table_notes:
a. Note 1: Including battle of Bassano and two combats.

b. Note 2: Including battle of Rivoli. Marched two nights and fought day between.

c. Note 3: Including maneuvers and most gallant fighting at Austerlitz.

d. Note 4: Carts to carry packs and men, turn and turn about.

title: Rates of Advance in Infantry Division Attacks in the Normandy-Northern France and Siegfried Line Campaigns
author: Wainstein, Leonard
organization: Institute for Defense Analyses, 400 Army-Navy Drive, Arlington, VA 22202
data_description:
a. The NORMANDY data are taken from Table 1 (page 12) of the source. The source obtained its information from official US Army histories and available archival records such as Daily Summaries, SITREPS, G1 Journals, etc.

b. (p v, Preface) "The research presented in this paper is in the area of historical combat statistics for possible use as input to simulation models. ... The purpose of this paper is not to attempt to establish precise relationships among the factors of rate of advance, casualties, resistance, and terrain. There is usually insufficient numerical data for that even on a one-sided basis. Rather it is hoped that some general relationships-some proportions-will emerge that will be of use to model-builders."

c. The data consists of a representative sample of 50 Allied infantry division attacks in which an advance of at least 300 yards was gained. Of these, 47 were by US and 3 by Canadian divisions. These occurred in Normandy-Northern France between mid-June and mid-August 1944 (except for two attacks in Cherbourg in early September). An indication of the terrain, degree of resistance, Allied strength, and battle casualties is included.

d. (p 1) "It should be stressed that many attacks fail to gain any ground, and these 90 advances were chosen because they did show an advance. Later, the approximate percent of all attacks in which advances occurred is determined." (p 15) "... I have arbitrarily considered that advances of under 300 yards represented no advance."

e. Distance is not defined, but presumably is FEBA displacement.

f. The time interval is defined as (p 10) "For simplicity's sake, a single day has been established as the base unit, despite the fact that in nearly every case the action lasted less than a full day and, for most actions, even less than the daylight period of the day. The purpose of the study is not to determine rates of advance on an hourly basis, but rather to determine the scale of the forward movement achieved in a good-sized sample."

g. (p 1) "Only bald statistics are presented, since, for purposes of statistical analysis and simulation, descriptive text on each battle really contributes little beyond some additional understanding of factors that cannot be quantified."

h. (p 5) "Terrain has been categorized as (1) open, (2) mixed, and (3) close or difficult. The word mixed thus includes the two commonly used descriptors, moderately open and moderately close, the distinction between which is really rather fine and essentially judgmental." (p 8) "... it is generally not possible to distinguish what proportion of an action occurred in a town versus the proportion that occurred on the open ground around it."

i. (pp 8-9, passim) "In the absence of German strength figures comparable to those obtainable for US units, degree of resistance rather than force ratio or enemy posture has been used as the descriptor for the enemy. ... The degree of enemy entrenchment-fortified position, prepared position, etc.-is not the best descriptor, since it is the fighting spirit of resistance maintained by the troops, as much as the strength of their position, that ultimately determines degree of resistance. ... In the Normandy cases, three simple categories of resistance are used: heavy, moderate, and light. For the Siegfried Line cases, five categories are used because the records employed a further breakdown of descriptor: heavy, moderate to heavy, moderate, light to moderate, and light.... The descriptor terms are those generally used in reference to the actions in the official histories. Yet in several cases the term used does not appear to accord with the casualties suffered. ... It is obvious that no standard measure exists for the relationship between degree of resistance and casualties ..."

j. (p 10) "While the actions listed all involved a single division, it should be understood that the entire division was not always involved. Attacks involving two or three regiments were most common, while single regiment attacks are also included, since they did represent an effort mounted by a division in which the division artillery and tank units invariably participated. There are also included cases where all three regiments or brigades attacked simultaneously, but divisional attacks using only a portion of the division were the norm. Battle really was a contest between regimental-sized units with their supporting elements."

k. (p 15) Based on "a hasty search," for the Normandy-Northern France area, 40 out of 371 division attack days showed "no" advance (i.e, advances of less than 300 yards). (p 20) For the Siegfried Line area, 17 out of 137 division attack days showed "no" advance.

l. (p 21) "The variations (in Tables 4 and 8) relating terrain type to degree of resistance are so marked that any average [relating rate of advance to degree of resistance] is highly questionable." Apparently Wainstein is here referring to the marked tendency for "heavy" resistance and "close" terrain to occur together. The combined cross-tabulation for all the data in this report is as follows, where we have collapsed the Siegfried Line resistance categories to three:

| Terrain class | Heavy | Moderate | Light | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open | 4 | 0 | 9 | 13 |
| Mixed | 13 | 17 | 14 | 44 |
| Close | 22 | 8 | 3 | 33 |
| Total | 39 | 25 | 26 | 90 |
discussion_and_comments:
a. The source table gives advances as "Actual or Daily Average of Advance." These we first converted into total distance advanced by multiplying by the duration of the action in days, and then into an average rate of advance per day by dividing by the number of days. The author's accompanying discussion of the quality of the data is sound, and suggests the care with which these data were assembled. However, in statistical terms, they are a "convenience sample" rather than a random one.

b. The limitation to advances of 300 yards or more is arbitrary and unfortunate. Also, it would have been better had the source given at least a general description of the portion of the division actually participating in the attacks.

c. The association between degree of resistance and terrain reinforces the suspicion that there is a pervasive systematic connection here-possibly due to the defender's tendency whenever possible to select "close/difficult" terrain for his most determined stands. An alternative is to postulate that attackers tend to perceive the resistance as heavy when the terrain is "close," i.e., that the association is caused by the vicious circle alluded to elsewhere. However, the latter postulate does imply a lack of professional objectivity in the attacker's perception of the situation that we are loathe to presume without good cause, although it is well known that even professionals can be victimized by such misperceptions from time to time.

d. In some cases, the original data table's dates spanned by the action are inconsistent with its durations in days. In such cases, we assumed that the dates were accurate and adjusted the durations accordingly. Note that some of the strength values in the original table were estimated, and that in one case the battle casualties are not for the same period as for the advance.

e. The source table gave advances as "Actual or Daily Average of Advance." These we first converted into total distance advanced by multiplying by the duration of the action in days, and then into an average rate of advance per day by dividing by the number of days.
data_table_notes: These apparently are advances by forces that were heavily engaged.

title: Opposed Rates of Advance of Large Forces in Europe (ORALFORE)
author: Dupuy, Trevor N. and Grace P. Hayes, et al.
organization: Historical Evaluation and Research Organization (HERO), prepared by HERO for the US Army Deputy Chief of Staff for Military Operations (DAMO-PLW) under Contract No. DAHC19-72-C-0015.
data_description:
a. The ORALFORE work was done (p 1, Introduction) "to provide insight into some of the basic problems of dealing with rates of advance in wargaming by attempting to ascertain whether historical combat experience provides a basis for calculating rates of advance of large forces (divisions and corps); by examining the assumption, accepted as valid in current models and wargames, that rates of advance can be related directly to the force ratios of opposing military forces; and by analyzing the factors that have influenced rates of advance in historical combat .... "

b. Specifically, the ORALFORE data were taken from those tables in the source entitled "Analysis of Rate of Advance of ... ," where the ellipsis stands for the name of the unit and the period concerned, e.g., "7th Panzer Division, 10-24 May 1940." These tables give data on the 14 advances listed below.

List of operations considered in ORALFORE

| Case no. | Short name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7th Panzer | Ardennes-Flanders Offensive, Ger 7th Panzer Division (Rommel), 20-24 May 40 |
| 2 | XLVII Corps | Orel to Moscow, Ger XLVII Corps, 13-30 Nov 41 |
| 3 | 18th Panzer | Orel to Moscow, Ger 18th Panzer Division, 13-23 Nov 41 |
| 4 | 29th Mtzd | Orel to Moscow, Ger 29th Motorized Division, 23 Nov-3 Dec 41 |
| 5 | XL Corps | Don River to Caucasus, Ger XL Panzer Corps, 21 Jul-23 Aug 42 |
| 6 | 3d Panzer | Don River to Caucasus, Ger 3d Panzer Division, 21 Jul-23 Aug 41 |
| 7 | VII Corps | Argentan to Liege, US VII Corps, 13 Aug-12 Sep 44 |
| 8 | 3d Armored | Argentan to Liege, US 3d Armored Division, 13 Aug-12 Sep 44 |
| 9 | 1st Inf | Argentan to Liege, US 1st Infantry Division, 13 Aug-8 Sep 44 |
| 10 | 9th Inf | Argentan to Liege, US 9th Infantry Division, 15 Aug-10 Sep 44 |
| 11 | XX Corps | Le Mans to Metz, US XX Corps, 14 Aug-13 Sep 44 |
| 12 | 7th Armored | Le Mans to Metz, US 7th Armored Division, 14 Aug-13 Sep 44 |
| 13 | XII Corps | Saar (Lorraine) Campaign, US XII Corps, 8 Nov-7 Dec 44 |
| 14 | 4th Armored | Saar (Lorraine) Campaign, US 4th Armored Division, 9 Nov-7 Dec 44 |

c. The source tables contain somewhat more detail than we chose to transcribe into our data base. We omitted those parts presenting force ratios computed in various ways (these depend upon many assumptions, extrapolations, and complicated procedures extraneous to the unvarnished historical record); estimates of how much of each day's advance distance was against negligible, slight, moderate, or intense opposition (the intensity categories are themselves subjective, and rating proportions of a day just compounds the subjectivity); air support present or absent (no evaluation of how much it was); logistics (data too sparse); and situation on flanks (given for advancing forces but not for defending forces).

d. The source gives additional information in its day-by-day narrative accounts of the action, and in its other tables (such as orders of battle, lists of weather conditions, etc.). Unfortunately, it was impractical to compress all of this information into data base form.

e. The source obtained its information from US and German documents in US archives, and selected books. However, "In some instances gaps in data could be filled by interpolation or extrapolation on the basis of professional military or historical experience."

f. "It proved to be impossible to complete the research and analysis for all six operations within the level of effort and the length of time provided. Problems of locating, translating, recording, and analyzing data consumed more time than was provided, with the result that some of the potential sources could not be completely exploited."

g. "The data immediately available for [the German Orel to Moscow Offensive] and [the German XL Panzer Corps, Don River to Caucasus] was not sufficient to permit calculation of the relative combat strengths of the opposing German and Russian forces. Nor was it possible within the limitations of this study to do the research in records of British and French forces necessary to secure accurate statistical information for [the German Ardennes-Flanders Offensive]. Consequently the analyses of these operations are based only on the information shown in the matrix. Also, because of changing corps boundaries, it has been necessary to study [the German Ardennes-Flanders Offensive] only from the point of view of the 7th Panzer Division. In [the German XL Panzer Corps, Don River to Caucasus] translation and detailed exploitation of records of the 3d Panzer Division has not been possible, and the analysis has been made entirely on the basis of XL Corps records."

h. For [the German XL Panzer Corps, Don River to Caucasus] (from p C-61): "No research has been done in Russian sources, and consequently it is not possible to include much information about the Russian strength and performance. Information on close air support on both sides appears to be incomplete. ... For much of this period German casualty data is available only for periods of five to ten days. The daily casualty figures used in the table, except where specific figures are available from other sources, are averages for these periods. ... Since Russian statistics were not available the force ratio has been estimated, with no attempt to do so on a daily basis. ... Since during most of the advance the active elements of the corps were two armored divisions, there is no significant difference in corps rates and division rates, save those caused by averaging of the rates of two different units."

i. "[The] intensity of opposition to advance is the historian's estimate from the narrative [account of the action], and from an assessment of relative casualties suffered on each side, of the tenacity of the defender's resistance to the attacker's advance on any given day. It bears no relationship to force ratio, but rather is an effort to reflect the interaction of those advancing and defending elements which were engaged on a given day—elements which were frequently only a relatively small fraction of the total forces available on both sides. Intensity of opposition to advance should not be confused with intensity of combat." Intensity of opposition is characterized as: intense, moderate, slight, negligible. But these terms are not defined in an objectively measurable way.

j. Weather is characterized as sunny, dry, dusty, warm, cool, rain, thunderstorm, good, etc. But these terms are not defined in an objectively measurable way.

k. Roadnet mobility is characterized as unlimited cross-country movement, good road net, fair road net, poor road net, impassable terrain. But these terms are not defined in an objectively measurable way.

l. Exceptional obstacles to advance is characterized as river, flooded area, fortified zone, exceptionally effective demolitions, urban area, sabotage by local populace, and desert. But these terms are not defined in an objectively measurable way.

m. Readiness condition is characterized as fresh, tired, weary, exhausted. But these terms are not defined in an objectively measurable way.

n. Defender's posture is characterized as hasty defense, fortified defense, position defense, delay, withdrawal. But these terms are not defined in an objectively measurable way.
discussion_and_comments:
a. The ORALFORE data were also used by U. Boddeker and J. Pantke in "Auswertung Historischer Konflikte zur Bestimmung von Vormarschraten [Evaluation of Historical Conflict for Determining Rates of Advance]," M-ZO 4013/08, Industrieanlagen-Betriebsgesellschaft mbH (IABG), Trier, West Germany, 20 April 1978.

b. Force ratios for the Ardennes-Flanders, Orel to Moscow, Don River to Caucasus, and Argentan to Liege operations were not evaluated within the scope of the ORALFORE work. The source states that "For Operations [US XX Corps, Le Mans to Metz] and [US XII Corps, Saar(Lorraine) Campaign] [the force ratios, relative combat effectiveness, relative mobility effectiveness, and intensity of combat] have been calculated by the Quantified Judgment Method (QJM)." Use and interpretation of the data on these operations should take this fact into account.

c. The meaning of many of the judgmental factors is uncertain. The ORALFORE report provides no objectively measurable criteria for such concepts as intensity of opposition, suitability of the weather for armor operations, quality of the roadnet, etc.

d. What ORALFORE intended by a "pause" is unclear. In at least one case (VII Corps), advances of 48 km are credited on each of 5 successive days even though both the attacker and the defender were categorized as having a pause (P) mission/posture on each of those days.

e. Observe that, from a statistical point of view, some of the information is correlated (i.e., partly redundant). This occurs because information on advances by divisions within a corps, as well as information on the corps' advance, are tabulated.

f. The characterization of intensity of opposition and of roadnet mobility may be circular. For example, a judgment that the roadnet was inadequate may inadvertently be influenced by the perceived slow rate of advance as much or more than by the "inherent" characteristics of the road net. Such vicious circles tend to crop up more often when characterizations are judgmental than when they are objectively measurable. The evaluation of readiness condition and defender's posture may also be circular.

g. The Soviet portions of these data can be compared to data on Soviet advances given elsewhere. See, for example, portions of the data bases CDB90, EASTFRON, GLANTZ, RADZIEV, RECORD, SAVKIN, and ROWLAND. See also HERO Combat Data Subscription Service (Volume I, No. 1, 1975; Volume II, No. 1, Winter 1976; Volume II, No. 3, 1977; and Volume II, No. 4, 1978). See also Losik, O. A. (ed.), "Organization and Tactical Employment of Soviet Tank Forces During the Great Patriotic War," Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defense, USSR, Moscow, 1979.

title: Statistical Analysis of Korean War Data—Spring 1951
author: Overholt, J. L.
organization: Center for Naval Analyses
numbers: Naval Warfare Analysis Group Study 64. Volume IX of the series of CNA reports on the "Study of Land/Air Tradeoffs (SLAT)"
data_description:
a. (p ix, Summary) "This volume [of the SLAT study series], concerned with the Korean War, describes attempts to relate the strengths of opposing U.N. North Korean/Chinese Communist forces, including fire support, with the ground gained and casualties on both sides. The objective is to determine, by statistical techniques, relationships among various kinds of battle data recorded each day by divisions. These were intended to provide guidance in the TWSP simulation ... "

b. (p ix, Summary) "The data for May 1951 is used because it is readily available and includes various kinds of combat in a period when sectors were relatively quiet, the thrust of the Chinese Communist Army near the Soyang River, and the counterattack of U.N. forces. In this period, there were no large break-throughs or amphibious landings."

c. (p ix, Summary) "The data consists of daily friendly and enemy strengths and casualties in the IX and X Corps in central Korea, air and artillery support of US and ROK divisions, and changes in territory. The enemy had no artillery or air support in this sector during this period. The data on small arms, machine guns, mortars, tanks, etc., though not available for either side in division records, is assumed to be proportional to the strengths and to such ordnance expended in World War II. Reserves were introduced continually by U.N. force, intermittently in the form of new divisions by the Communists."

d. Official after-action reports and operational summaries were used as the principal data sources.

e. Distance is defined as (p 7) "The ground gained (in area) was measured by planimeter from the change that occurred from one day to the next for each division. We obtained the average gain or loss by dividing the area by the front length." However, the source's Annex D-1 describes the "Variables Used in the Regression Analysis" as "the territory measured in square kilometers acquired or relinquished by a friendly unit during the time period under consideration." and expresses the value used in the regressions as this value divided by 10.

f. The time interval is defined as daily intervals (presumably starting around midnight).

g. (p 11) Fire support refers to the artillery and air ordnance delivered in support of each division. Light artillery is expressed in numbers of rounds of ammunition 105mm and larger. Artillery support to divisions, in tons per mile of front.

h. (pp 11-13) Data were collected on three types of air support: close air support, sorties by light bombers, and sorties by heavy bombers. Close air support consists of ordnance sorties delivered under ground or air control to targets beyond the forward bomb line. The ordnance delivered by light bombers within 15 miles of the battle line in support of each division was taken as fire in support of ground troops. Data were also obtained on ordnance delivered in support of corps and army. Heavy bomber support consists of B-29 sorties supporting the divisions, corps, and army.

i. (p 21) "The battles are described by [the] variables already mentioned—the strengths, casualties, and firepower of the opposing sides—and such others as weather, terrain, tempo of fighting, the effects of pre-bombardment and of movement of adjacent units, and the decisions of the opposing commanders to attack, withdraw, or hold."
discussion_and_comments:
a. This is a major and apparently one of the earliest efforts to obtain enough detailed data on real combat operations to compare them to the results of wargames. The importance of such efforts is clear.

b. (p i, Abstract) "Though the work is indicative, it is limited by the poor quality of information about enemy strength." (p 7) "Enemy strength was measured from the order of battle, as derived by intelligence sources. Only the elements of the Communist division opposing each friendly division are available." (p 11) "The enemy strength data was poor. The order of battle was derived from captured prisoners; when the enemy was attacking, little or no data was available because no prisoners were taken. Even where such intelligence was available, it was often inaccurate because the enemy troops were sometimes transferred and did not know the designations of their new units when interrogated. Analysis after the war disclosed that the number of enemy troops was frequently underestimated because the Chinese Communists were trained for long night marches, averaging 15 to 20 miles a night for two or three weeks, and were taught to stand stock-still when aircraft were heard or sighted. U.N. forces discounted sightings by South Korean civilians. Finally, known enemy casualties were not subtracted from the order of battle. [In one of the author's attempts to improve the quality of enemy strength information] simple subtraction of casualties from strength figures led to inconsistencies." (p 46) "The enemy strength and casualty data should be examined more critically to see whether estimates are made in the same manner by various forces. Apparently the 2nd Army Division estimated greater casualties than the 1st Marine Division. The casualties may be [i.e., may have been] estimated from the quantity of ordnance fired and may be fallacious."
data_table_notes: This report presents its data only in graphical form. Consequently, specific values are no longer readily recoverable. Unfortunately, it was not feasible in the course of this work to convert it back into digital (tabular or numerical) form. Accordingly, no data table is provided for this data source. However, the source is cited for the sake of completeness.

title: Military Unit Rates of Advance in Attack
author: Parsons, LTC Norman W.
organization: Combat Operations Research Group
available_from: Wainstein, Leonard, "An Examination of the Parsons and Hulse Papers on Rates of Advance," Paper P-991, Institute for Defense Analyses, December 1973, AD-779 848
data_description:
a. (p A-2) "It has seemed apparent that there is a general lack of information regarding the actual rates of advance of military units in an attack against an enemy. This lack of information has been noticed in map problems presented in various service schools and in war games and battle planning activities. It seems that in the majority of cases the rate of advance of an attacking unit is considered to approximate the rate of movement in an administrative march cross country, without consideration for the various types of terrain included in the general term 'cross country.' Casual examination of narrative accounts of military operations indicates that such a rate of advance is unrealistically high. It is believed that more accurate knowledge of factual rates of advance is required in order to permit more realistic map problems and battle plans. [Accordingly, in this paper] the problem is to determine the rates of advance of infantry units in attack under various conditions of terrain and enemy resistance."

b. The source provides data on 33 examples of successful attacks by infantry battalion-sized forces supported by artillery and tanks. Apparently successful attacks are those that reached their intended objective (cf. para d, below). Unsuccessful attacks were not tabulated, although p A-2 remarks that "It should be noted that [in the records consulted] there were many unsuccessful attacks by the same units in the same general terrain and against the same general types of enemy resistance. This analysis does not consider the probability of success of any given attack under the conditions tabulated." Of the 33 examples, 3 are from Guadalcanal, 10 are from Italy, and 20 are from NW Europe (specifically, 14 from the Cherbourg Peninsula/St. Lo region, and 6 from the Moselle River/Huertgen Forest region).

c. The source obtained its information from various Deptartment of the Army History Division reports, and military intelligence reports of the War Department.

d. Distance is defined as (p 4) "The analysis considers only the average rates of advance from the line of departure to the objective when the attack was successful."

e. Terrain is defined as open (lightly wooded, slightly rolling, elevation changes less than 30 meters per mile and not more than 25 percent woods cover); moderately open (wooded and rolling, elevation changes 30 to 50 meters per mile or 25 to 50 percent woods cover); moderately close (wooded and hilly, elevation changes 80 to 100 meters per mile or 50 to 75 percent woods cover); or mountainous (elevation changes over 300 meters per mile)

f. Type action is defined as river crossing, regimental attack, etc., and as "Administrative," "Pursuit," "Exploitation of a Breakthrough," "Seizure of a Deep Objective," or "Attack Through Infantry out of a Bridgehead."

g. Artillery support is defined as number of battalions.

h. Enemy strength and resistance is the number of enemy units (battalions, companies, etc.) if that is known; otherwise it is categorized as light, none, very heavy, etc.

i. Weather is defined as cold, rainy, clear, etc.

j. (p 2) "Other factors which have a bearing on rates of movement, such as morale, fatigue, extent of prior planning and reconnaissance, amount of preparation and briefing, and similar items, although having important effects, cannot be separated for consideration because of the lack of data."
discussion_and_comments:
a. This supplements the HULSE data base on armored unit rates of advance by providing information on infantry unit rates of advance. The values here are mainly for forces that were heavily engaged.

b. (p 3) "In studying Table 3 there is some suspicion that the description of the enemy resistance may include some element of description of the difficulties of the terrain." If so, this gives rise to the vicious circle described in our discussion of the BAORG data base. It is also possible that the defender may choose to defend more strongly at places where the terrain is difficult. Either deliberate defender choice or the vicious circle would induce a statistical confounding and correlation of the degree of enemy resistance with the difficulty of the terrain.

title: A Survey of "Quick Wins" in Modern War
author: HERO
organization: Historical Evaluation and Research Organization
data_description:
a. (p 1, Introduction) "In an attempt to identify the factors which seem to have contributed to, or militated against, rapid and decisive victory, the Historical Evaluation and Research Organization (HERO) has studied seven examples of 'quick wins' in modern war, three examples of 'almost quick wins' and three examples that ended in stalemate." Distances and durations are given for 30 occasions described as "major rapid offensives" of the 19th and 20th centuries. The principal means of movement in these offensives are also given.

b. The major rapid offensives studied are Marengo, Ulm, Jena, Friedland, Danube, Russia, Lutzen-Bautzen, Vicksburg, Savannah-Raleigh, Appomattox, Sadowa, Metz-Sedan, Marne, Caparetto, Third Gaza, Megiddo, Flanders, Barbarossa, Malaya, Luzon I, Caucasus, Cobra, Luzon II, Manchuria, N. Korean Offensive, UN Offensive, Sinai Campaign, Samaria, and Golan.

c. (p 2) "Only secondary sources are used because time did not permit consulting primary documents. Consequently statistical data is incomplete and may, in some instances, be questionable." Just what secondary sources were used is not reported. Nevertheless, the source contains many tabulations and charts, and includes a chapter entitled "Quantitative Analysis." So apparently the values were considered sufficiently trustworthy to be reported in quantitative form.

d. We took the QUICKWIN data from the source's Figure 5. It does not say where it obtained its information, but apparently it is from a variety of sources. Their presentation in a single table implies that they are on a roughly comparable basis.

e. Distance is defined as (p 20) "[After preparing the narrative accounts] distances advanced during the campaign, or during the critical period of the campaign, were then determined for selected units (or as an average of the force as a whole, whichever seemed most reasonable and was facilitated by the availability of suitable data and maps)." What defines the duration of the campaign—or of its "critical period"—is unspecified. Tabulated values are characterized as "Total Distance Considered," which in three cases (Russia, Barbarossa, and Malaya) differs from other values characterized as "Total Distance in Campaign." No indication is given as to whether the distance is "for selected units" or is instead "an average of the force as a whole."

f. Time interval is not defined, but is characterized as "Days in Campaign," or as "Days to Decision." For 21 of the 30 operations, these time intervals coincide, and in nine they differ. In six of the nine instances where they differ, rates are based on the days to decision, but in three instances rates are based on the days in campaign. The source does not comment on these differences.

g. Several situational descriptors are used (e.g., "weapons quality," "political involvement," "simplicity," etc.), but these are not defined in an objectively measurable way.
discussion_and_comments:
a. It is hard to tell just what the source means by many of its descriptors, such as "preponderance of effective force strength." Also, it is hard to judge the extent to which the values assigned to these descriptors are post hoc, and hence are affected by the vicious circle referred to elsewhere. The key question is whether those values were or could have been foretold before the campaign was conducted, rather than being based on after-the-fact knowledge of the campaign's results. Leadership and planning are prime examples. If the campaign turns out badly for side A, that is strong evidence that side A's planning and/or leadership were faulty. But evidently before the campaign was conducted side A considered its planning and leadership to be adequate—for otherwise it would have changed them. Other examples could be cited, but the point is clear.

b. In several cases, the time intervals presented in the source's Figure 5 (which is a table giving, among other things, the dates, time intervals, distances, and rates of advance for the operations studied) do not agree with the starting and ending dates given in the same table. In our data base, the rates have been recalculated by assuming the distances and the start-end dates to be accurate.

c. In Figure 5 of the source, the column labeled "Distance, km/day" clearly should read "Average Rate of Advance, km/day."

d. The average rate of advance shown for Appomattox and for Malaya in Figure 5 of the source are incorrect (i.e., not consistent with the distance and duration cited there). To two significant digits, they should read 17 and 18 km/day, respectively. For our work, we assumed that the distances and start-end dates were accurate and computed elapsed times and rates from them, rather than use those in the original tabulations.

e. A tabulation very similar to that of the source's Figure 5 is given in Figure 8 of the Breakthrough report ("A Study of Breakthrough Operations," HERO, October 1976, Historical Evaluation and Research Organization, AD-A036 492). In fact, the Breakthrough report gives distances, durations, and rates of advance for exactly the same 30 campaigns as the source. In the Breakthrough report, the average rates of advance for Appomattox and Malaya are given correctly. However, there are other discrepancies between these two tabulations, as indicated in the list of examples below. Neither paper comments on these differences, although presumably they arise partly from considering different portions of the campaigns. Since the "days to breakthrough" values of the Breakthrough paper are usually only a small fraction of the days elapsed from the start to the end of the campaign, it is hard to tell just what part of the campaign the Breakthrough tabulation represents. In our work, we used the distances and (corrected) durations from the source. Using the alternative values from the Breakthrough report would not materially affect our results.

Examples of discrepancies between the Quick Wins and Breakthrough data

| Operation | Values in Breakthrough | Values in Quick Wins |
|---|---|---|
| Megiddo | 70/2 = 35* | 310/14 = 22 |
| Flanders | 10/2 = 5 | 545/26 = 21 |
| Cobra | 21/3 = 7 | 880/32 = 28 |
| Manchuria | 160/8 = 20 | 450/12 = 38 |
| North Korean Offensive | 50/3 = 17 | 560/42 = 13 |
| Jitra (Malaya) | 10/1 = 10 | 515/32 = 16 |

\* Distance (km) / Time (days) = Rate (km/day)

f. We also found similar occasional discrepancies between the QUICKWIN data and those reported for ostensibly the same operations in Dupuy, Trevor N., "Analysing Trends in Ground Combat," *History, Numbers and War: A HERO Journal*, Vol. 1, No. 2, Summer 1977, pp 77-91, and Dupuy, Trevor N., "A Fallacy of American Combat Simulations: Rates of Advance are NOT Proportional to Force Ratios," *History, Numbers and War: A HERO Journal*, Vol. 1, No. 2, Summer 1977, pp 103-114.
data_table_notes: Presumably these advances are by forces that were but lightly engaged.

title: Tankovii Udar [Tank Attack: Tank Armies in Offensive Operations of the Fronts According to the Experience of the Great Patriotic War] (in Russian)
author: Radzievskii, Professor General of the Army Aleksii Ivanov
organization: Order of the Workers of the Red Banner, Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defence, Moscow
data_description:
a. The data are taken from the source's Appendix 3 "Selected Indices of Offensive Operations of Tank Armies in the Years 1943-1945." This gives the "Maximum Speed of Advance" for several operations. However, the source does not define exactly what is meant by that.

b. The source provides copious references to the Archives of the USSR Ministry of Defense. But it does not say exactly where it obtained its information on maximum speeds of advance.
discussion_and_comments: Some portions of these data can be compared to data on Soviet advances given elsewhere. See, for example, portions of the data bases CDB90, EASTFRON, GLANTZ, ORALFORE, RECORD, SAVKIN, and ROWLAND. See also HERO Combat Data Subscription Service (Volume I, No. 1, 1975; Volume II, No. 1, Winter 1976; Volume II, No. 3, 1977; and Volume II, No. 4, 1978). See also Losik, O. A. (ed.), "Organization and Tactical Employment of Soviet Tank Forces During the Great Patriotic War," Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defense, USSR., Moscow, 1979.
data_table_notes: The rates given in this table are maximum rates.

title: The Rate of Advance of the Front Line in Some World War II Campaigns
author: Mulholland, R. P., and R. D. Specht
organization: The RAND Corporation
data_description:
a. Motivated by issues arising in wargames, this document aims to present some historical data on the velocity of the frontline and strengths of the opposing forces in the European and Mediterranean Theaters of World War II.

b. The specific operations studied are:

1. Sicly, D to D+30
2. Salerno to Winter Line (Italy), D to D+60
3. First US Army, Normandy to St. Lo, D to D+40
4. Battle of the Bulge, D to D+40
5. First US Army, Breakout to the Westwall, D to D+120
6. Seventh US Army, October 1944 to February 1945, D to D+150
7. European Theater of Operations, D to D+300

c. The source obtained its data from (p 9) "These data are taken from the After Action Reports and Histories of the various Allied Armies and from other documents listed in the Bibliography."

d. Distance is defined as (p 9) "Rates of advance are estimated from the situation maps of the campaigns."

e. Time interval is not defined. What calendar dates the authors intended to include in their intervals from D to D + (whatever) are never explicitly stated.

f. (pp 8-9) "We ignore terrain, climate, initiative, logistic support, air support, the tactical situation, quality of personnel and equipment, mobility, etc., and seek such gross relation as may exist merely between the Allied and Axis strengths and the rate of advance of the battle line. The strength of each side is measured by the number of equivalent divisions in the line; this number is corrected by such numerical values for manpower and estimates of equivalent strength as we could find."
discussion_and_comments:
a. This is an important study, and it appears to be the first to propose a specific functional relation, founded upon historical analysis rather than speculation, for the effect of force ratio upon rate of advance.

b. The manner in which equivalent strengths are obtained is somewhat obscure. Apparently, the number of divisions "in line" on each side was used, unless information suggesting a modification of that value to yield "equivalent divisions" was available. The operations studied are very large indeed, so the strength appears to be that for the entire theater, while the advances would appear to be those of the leading elements only. Accordingly, unless carefully justified, the results should not be "scaled down" to lower echelons, such as divisions, brigades and battle groups, or battalions.

c. Some of the data are correlated (i.e., partly redundant). For example, the advance in the European Theater of Operations, D to D+300 depended on the results of operations 2b(3) through 2b(6), and so is hardly independent of them.
data_table_notes: This report presents its data only in graphical form. Consequently, specific values are no longer readily recoverable. Unfortunately, it was not feasible in the course of this work to convert it back into digital (tabular or numerical) form. Accordingly, no data table is provided for this data source. However, the source is cited for the sake of completeness.

title: Armored Advance Rates: A Historical Inquiry
author: Record, Jeffrey
organization: Military Review, pp 63-72
data_description:
a. This article's purpose is to question the validity of Soviet General Staff Guidelines calling for sustained rates of advance of 70 miles per day.

b. The operations studied include:

- (1) German XIX Corps from Border to Channel, May 1941
- (2) German 2nd Panzer Group from start of Barbarossa to Smolensk, June 1941
- (3) German Afrika Korps, advance to Mersa Matruh, June 1942
- (4) British 8th Army, El Alamein Offensive, October 1942
- (5) US Third Army from Avranches to Troyes, August 1944
- (6) Israeli units in Six-Day War, June 1967

c. The source obtained its information from various history books, which are cited in its bibliography.

d. Environmental and operational factors such as how the distances and elapsed times are defined, what weather, terrain, and degree of enemy resistance are not specified. However, presumably enemy resistance was slight to negligible.
discussion_and_comments:
a. The evidence presented is largely anecdotal and cannot serve as a basis for overgeneralization or overextrapolation.

b. Some of the Soviet operations in these data can be compared to data on Soviet advances given elsewhere. See, for example, portions of the data bases CDB90, EASTFRON, GLANTZ, ORALFORE, RADZIEV, SAVKIN, and ROWLAND. See also HERO Combat Data Subscription Service (Volume I, No. 1, 1975; Volume II, No. 1, Winter 1976; Volume II, No. 3, 1977; and Volume II, No. 4, 1978). See also the SIMPKIN note in Appendix B, and Losik, O. A. (ed.), "Organization and Tactical Employment of Soviet Tank Forces During the Great Patriotic War," Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defense, USSR, Moscow, 1979.

title: Research Study on Predictive War Game Factors: Final Report
author: Cockrell, James K., and Donn Carter
organization: RMC Research Corporation
numbers: Prepared for SHAPE Technical Centre, Contract C.72-03
data_description:
a. The source's data sets were assembled by a study team led by Mr. James Cockrell of the RMC Research Corporation's RMC Systems Group, supported by one or more contracts with the SHAPE Technical Centre (STC), and carried out under the guidance of Dr. Rex Goad of STC. (p 1, Introduction) "The purpose of the effort was to produce data and algorithms that can be used in SHAPE computer war games to predict the outcome of engagements between ground units in non-nuclear war situations. Outcome measures were to be distance advanced and primary resource attrition suffered in 24-hour periods."

b. The data are from two major operations, as described below.

- (1) The Ardennes Data Set. The Ardennes data set is described by the source as being for a nominal 24-hour period and a nominal division level (actually brigade to division size) on the attacking side. Advances were measured as the maximum penetrations achieved and held during approximately 24-hour periods. The Ardennes data set consists of a total of 150 attack days (49 US attacking German, 15 US attacking German with a German counterattack, 73 German attacking US, and 13 German attacking US with a US counterattack). In each case the attacker was confronted by a defense in place, as opposed to a delay. All of these actions took place during the first 18 days (16 December 1944 to 2 January 1945) of the Ardennes Campaign of WWII (Battle of the Bulge). For this part of our data base we used the source's table on pages B-6 through B-9 of its Appendix B.
- (2) The Lorraine Data Set. Appendix B of the source states that the data collection process used for the Lorraine data set was the same as for the Ardennes data set. The Lorraine data set consists of 100 attack days (63 US attacking German, 19 US attacking German with a German counterattack, 9 German attacking US, 9 German attacking US with a US counterattack). All of these actions took place between 8 September and 27 November 1944 in eastern France. For this part of our data base we used the source's table on pages E-17 through E-19 of its Appendix E.

c. (p 7) "The US National Archives Captured Records Center was the primary source for German unit records and other documents. These included microfilmed copies of unit operational records, war maps, and results of interviews or responses from captured German division, corps, and army commanders and staff officers. ... For US battle day information the primary source was the National Records Center of the Archives. After action reports, daily and other periodic reports, journal files, histories, and order of battle studies from Army level down to battalion level were examined to establish the composition, location, disposition, mission and activity of the units of interest." For the Ardennes data set, supplemental mobility and visibility information apparently were collected by Cockrell and his colleagues in the early 1970s by visiting the site of the battle at the corresponding time of year and making visibility and maneuverability estimates (see the source's p 155). (p 69) "The terrain analysis for the Lorraine data set was made without the benefit of a terrain reconnaissance and is not considered to be as accurate as is that used in the Ardennes data sample."

d. (p B-2) "Attack missions were coded as obtained from recorded mission statements. Limited objective attacks or counterattacks which were considered to have been limited by mission considerations rather than by resources were not included in the sample (emphasis added). For example, an attack clearly conducted to restore the frontline would not be included. Also left out were any reported attacks where there appeared to be significant question as to whether an attack was really made." (p 6) "... it was important to avoid 'pseudo attacks' and delaying actions in which the results of a day's actions were dictated by considerations other than an attack mission opposed by a defense mission."

e. Distance is defined as (p B-5) "Advances were measured to within 100 meters from the line occupied by the defense when the day's fighting began-that is, only penetration distance was counted, not advance-to-the-assault-position distance." (pp 67-68) "Many days in which there were division attacks during this period [Lorraine Campaign] could not be included in the data set because there was insufficient data on either the German or the US force, or there was evidence that a German defending force had withdrawn rather than attempting to defend its positions against a US attack. (Whenever an attack struck a defended position to which the defender had withdrawn, the ensuing battle was recorded from that point on, as if the attack had begun at that point-as long as this did not occur toward the end of a day of attacker movement, because it was observed that in such cases the attack was usually not continued long after dark.)"

f. Time intervals are defined as (p 6) "These [data collection and other considerations] combined to indicate a nominal 24-hour period and a nominal division level on the attack force side as natural separation points."

g. The source data include such situational descriptors as the sector of the front, the date, the attacker's strength in number of infantry platoon equivalents, tank strength, antitank firepower, artillery firepower, personnel casualties, tank and tank-equivalent losses, visibility, mobility, attacker and defender postures or missions, and the distance advanced. The technical definitions and detailed codes used to describe all these items are too complex to summarize readily. See the RMC report and the Data Table Notes below for details.
discussion_and_comments:
a. This study represents a major effort to assemble a substantial data base, and to apply powerful multivariate statistical analysis methods to extract from it solid relationships that could be used to model attrition and advance rates in wargames and simulations. Its data are for forces that were heavily engaged.

b. (p 73) "The indication that [the Lorraine] data set is not taken from the same population as the Ardennes set may be the result of data errors. It was found during the long series of regressions using the Ardennes set that data errors are difficult to identify and that the best indicator of error is peculiar behavior of regression results -analysis of these then leads back to particular elements of the data and rigorous reexamination then frequently exposes errors. It was not possible to perform any such analyses on the [Lorraine] data set because of contract fund limitations, and it is likely that at least some of the difference between the two sets is due to the [Lorraine] data set not having been 'shaken down'." However, this process could also focus attention on errors in the "non-fitting" data values to the exclusion of errors in the "fitting" data-a focus on Type I errors to the neglect of Type II errors.

c. Some portion of the attacks were night attacks (cf. p 16 and p 20), but this information has not been recorded in the RMC report (except through the Visibility codes, which are surrogates for many different kinds of visibility-degrading conditions). The source observes that the Germans conducted night attacks substantially more often than did the US. Hence, the visibility conditions are statistically confounded with the side attacking.

d. The general character of the Lorraine and Ardennes campaigns differs in three principal ways.

- (1) In the Lorraine campaign, troops were less concentrated on both sides, resulting in more isolated battles rather than in linear front action.
- (2) Water courses in the Lorraine area at the time were flooded and limited the movement of tanks to captured or erected bridges. Infantry were less restricted. In the Ardennes, tank movement was significantly less restricted most of the time.
- (3) A higher percentage of brigade-size attack forces occur in the Lorraine data set than in the Ardennes data set.

e. The following works summarize and/or analyze various aspects of the source data.

- (1) Goad, Rex, "Prediction of Opposed Movement and Casualty Rates," SHAPE Technical Centre, Professional Paper, STC-PP-75, July 1973.
- (2) Cockrell, James K., "Prediction of Advances in Ground Combat," Conference on Modelling Land Battle Systems for Military Planning, Ottobrun, Germany, 1974.
- (3) Goad, Rex, "Predictive Equations for Opposed Movement and Casualty Rates for Land Forces," SHAPE Technical Centre, STC-PP-90, The Hague, Netherlands, August 1974, AD-921 726.
- (4) Goad, Rex, "The Modelling of Movement in Tactical Games," Professional Paper STC PP-158, Operations Research Division, SHAPE Technical Centre, The Hague, April 1979. (Also published in Operational Research Games for Defense, edited by Reiner K. Huber, Klaus Niemeyer, and Hans W. Hoffmann, R. Oldenburg, Munich and Vienna, 1979.)
- (5) Lindley, D. V. and A. M. Skeene, "Predictive Relationships for Opposed Movement and Casualty Rates for Land Forces." unpublished memorandum from Department of Statistics and Computer Science, University College of London, to Dr. Rex Goad of the SHAPE Technical Centre, 24 January 1976.
- (6) Schaffer, Alfred, "Determination of the Functional Relation Between the Speeds of Movement and the Loss-Ratios of Military Units in Battle," Graduate Dissertation, ID No. 03-77, Hochschule der Bundeswehr, München, 9 June 1977.
data_table_notes:
a. ID is the sector identification code used by RMC.

b. DATE is the date of the action.

c. ATTACK TYPE CODE is as follows:

- 0 = A US main attack as part of a continuing offensive
- 1 = A German attack as part of a continuing offensive
- 6 = A German attack combined with a US counterattack
- 7 = A US attack combined with a German counterattack

ATTACK DESCRIP is an alphabetical description of the ATTACK TYPE CODE.

d. POSTURE CODE applies to the defender, and is as follows:

- 5 = frontline troops in well dug-in positions with at least some overhead cover: an organized, well-prepared defensive position
- 6 = frontline troops in foxholes with all heavy weapons dug-in
- 7 = Some elements of the defense as in Level 6, and a significant portion not well dug-in or organized
- 8 = A hasty defense in which there has not been opportunity to organize the defense or to dig in. This level was also used for "meeting engagements" (i.e., an attack meeting a counterattack, two attacks colliding, etc.)

This procedure was adopted since there was no known method of quantifying the relative worth of each posture level. Thus, the code merely identifies the type posture level for each day.

e. ATTACKER/DEFENDER CODE is as follows:

- 1 = A US-initiated attack (i.e., Attack Type Code = 0 or 7)
- 2 = A German-initiated attack (i.e., Attack Type Code = 1 or 6)

f. ARTY US is the number of rounds of US artillery ammunition expended in close (direct support) of that sector on that date.

g. ARTY GER is coded as follows:

- 1 = low intensity of German artillery
- 2 = moderate intensity of German artillery
- 3 = high intensity of German artillery
- 4 = very high intensity of German artillery

h. Four environment codes are given. The first pair ("ENV LINE" or E1 and E2) are mobility restrictions and visibility ranges in the area of the defensive position. The second pair ("ENV PEN" or E3 and E4) are these same conditions along the axis of penetration. Visibility is the range to which the defender could put well-directed fire on the attacker along the approaches available to the attacker. Mobility is the extent to which all factors combined to hinder the mobility of the attacker.

The codes used for E1 and E3 are:

- 0 = No restriction on infantry or tank movement
- 1 = Infantry unrestricted, tanks canalized
- 2 = Infantry unrestricted, tanks severely canalized
- 3 = Infantry unrestricted, tanks must breach
- 4 = Infantry canalized, tanks canalized
- 5 = Infantry canalized, tanks severely canalized
- 6 = Infantry canalized, tanks must breach
- 7 = Infantry canalized, tanks difficult to breach
- 8 = Infantry must breach, tanks must breach
- 9 = Infantry and tanks difficult to breach

The codes used for E2 and E4 are:

- 1 = Not over 100 meters visibility range generally available
- 2 = Not over 300 meters visibility range generally available
- 3 = Not over 1000 meters visibility range generally available
- 4 = Well over 1000 meters visibility range generally available.

i. INF PLTN is an index of the infantry resources available, based on the number of infantry platoons contained in each unit or fraction of a unit listed as being involved in each attack day. A computer program calculated the number of infantry platoons contained in each unit or fraction of a unit listed as being involved in each battle day (i.e., the battalions, etc., listed in the source's Annex A). It did this by using organizational information about each type of unit (e.g., a US parachute infantry battalion contains nine infantry platoons, etc.).

j. ARMOR is the number of tank-like vehicles available, including tanks, assault guns, self-propelled tank destroyers, and German self-propelled antitank guns (Jagdpanzers).

k. ANTIARMOR is a weighted average number of antiarmor weapons using the following weights.

Antitank Weapon System Weighting Factor for the RMC Data

| Weapon system | Weighting factor |
|---|---|
| 2-in to 3-in AT rocket launcher (Bazooka or Panzerfaust) | 0.10 |
| 37mm AT or light tank gun | 0.12 |
| 57mm AT gun | 0.41 |
| 76mm AT or medium tank gun | 0.70 |
| 90mm AT or heavy tank gun | 0.79 |

l. MECZ CODE is the percentage of infantry in the attacking or in the defending force that was mechanized, divided by 10. E.g., an entry of "4" means that 40 percent of the infantry in the force were mechanized.

m. TANK ATTN is the total armor loss rate per thousand armor vehicles per day.

n. PERS ATTN is the personnel battle casualty rate per thousand personnel per day, and is computed on the basis of 40 men per infantry platoon.

o. ADV DIST is measured in units of kilometers, to an accuracy of 0.1 km, from the line occupied by the defense when the day's fighting began. That is, only penetration distance was counted, not advance-to-the-assault-position distance.

p. FRONTAGE is an estimate of the length in kilometers of the part of the frontline which was attacked in each battle day-not merely the points of close contact, but the length of the front the defending force had to protect as a direct result of the attacking force's actions and immediate capabilities.

q. Special note on the Lorraine data set: the listing of the Lorraine data set is identical in format to that of the Ardennes data set. However, as noted in the source, its content differs in that some of the Lorraine data set columns are not complete. This is because the results of RMC's analysis of the Ardennes data set indicated that those data items would not be needed in the Lorraine data set, and at this point in RMC's study available resources would not support any additional work beyond the minimum necessary to complete the effort. Furthermore, in the Lorraine data set the vision-range coding did not attempt to discriminate between the 2 and 3 codes (100-300 meters and 300-700 meters) because this degree of detail would not be recognized in the dummy coding used, and it was hard to obtain from map data.

title: The Pace of Operations: Maximum Rates of Advance
author: Rowland, David, and David Watson
organization: Defense Operational Analysis Establishment (UK)
data_description:
a. The source's aim is define the upper limits of advance rate for unopposed movement. In support of this aim it provides data on a wide variety of operations including several from the 19th Century, the Boer War, WWII, the Falklands War of 1982, and others too numerous to name.

b. The source does not indicate where it obtained its information.

c. Environmental and operational factors such as how the distances and elapsed times are defined, what weather, terrain, and degree of enemy resistance are not usually specified. However, presumably enemy resistance was slight to negligible.
discussion_and_comments: As indicated by its title, the source considers only advances by forces that are lightly engaged. The source is a preliminary or working paper, so its findings may be modified in the final version. But it contains a wealth of data not readily available from any other source.
data_table_notes:
a. Note 1: The advances of May 16th and May 17th were, in fact, one single advance ending at 0515 on the latter date, some 70.4 miles (113.30 km) having been covered in about 19 1/4 hours, for a rate of advance of about 141.26 km/day.

b. Note 2: Lidell Hart, in "The Rommel Papers," remarks that the advance of 17 June "far exceeded any day's advance which had ever been made in warfare."

c. Note 3: Harriet Fast Scott disputes Soviet claims as to (1) intensity of opposition, (2) distance displaced, (3) size of force displaced. She speculates that Soviet motives were to claim as much territory as possible in preparation for postwar negotiations.

d. Note 4: To Camilla Creek House. The time 0700 is based on the map in MG John Frost, "2 Para, Falklands," and perhaps represents the time at which the whole battalion arrived. Some elements reached Camilla Creek House earlier. Max Hastings, in "The Battle for the Falklands," says that the "red torch signal" signifying D-Company's arrival was seen at 0300, and the RMO, Captain Hughes talks in Max Arthur's "Above All, Courage," of a march of "six hours and fourteen kilometers."

e. Note 5: It seems that both 45 Commando and 3 Para set out with the men carrying about 120 pounds each. After the first two-days' march, the Commandos switched to "heavy fighting order," which seems to have ranged from about 76 to 83 pounds. Martin Middlebrook in his "Operation Corporate" says that the Paras in general carried lighter weights than the Marines (presumably similar to the "heavy fighting order"). Captain J. H. McManners RA, in a March 1983 letter in the RUSI Journal, makes a distinction between Marine "yomping"--"a rather onamotopoetic word--used when distances have to be covered and all resources have to be carried by the individual on his own back," and "tabbing"--which is short for "tactical advance for battle."

f. Note 6: Landing near Depienne, Tunisia, on 29 November, the Bn advanced toward Oudna, becoming involved in heavy fighting over the next 2 days. On 1 December, having suffered heavy casualties and still pursued by the Germans, the paratroopers retreated, reaching Medjez el Bab on 3 December.

title: Tempy Nastupleniya [Rates of Advance] (in Russian)
author: Savkin, COL Vasiliv Yefisovich
organization: Military Publishing House, Ministry of Defense, Moscow
data_description:
a. The SAVKIN data are taken from the appendix of the source. The origins of these data are not identified, but appear to be based on a variety of Soviet military history studies.

b. The source provides distances, durations, and average rates of advance for 81 operations conducted by the Soviet Red Army in World War II, grouped into four periods or phases of the war. The first period includes the defense of Moscow and other actions of 1941 and 1942. The second period includes the defense of Stalingrad and other actions in 1942 and 1943. The third period includes the major Soviet offensives on their western front in 1944 and 1945. The fourth period includes the Soviet offensives in the Far East conducted in 1945.
discussion_and_comments:
a. Some of the source's rates of advance do not agree with the stated distances and elapsed times. For our work, we assumed that the distances and elapsed times were correct, and recomputed the rates from them.

b. All of the source's data are for operations in which the Soviet Red Army was victorious. It gives no data on Soviet retreats, such as occurred during Germany's initial invasion of the Soviet Union under Operation Barbarossa.

c. The source does not give the details of terrain, principal means of locomotion, or degree of enemy opposition. While Savkin's text may shed some light on these factors, it is in Russian and no English translation of it seems to be available.

d. The source's data for the Manchurian campaign are (with one exception) identical to those given in Appendix 3 of Glantz, LTC David M., "August Storm: The Soviet 1945 Strategic Offensive in Manchuria," Leavenworth Papers No. 7, US Army Command and General Staff College, Fort Leavenworth, KS, February 1983. The exception is that the source omits the Cav-Mech Group's advance on the Trans-Baikal Front, reported in Glantz as 4255 km/day). Glantz, in turn, obtained his information from "The Campaign of the Soviet Armed Forces in the Far East in 1945: Facts and Figures," Military History Journal (Soviet), August 1945, Table 6.
data_table_notes: These advances presumably are mainly by forces that were only lightly engaged.

title: Rates of Advance in Infantry Division Attacks in the Normandy-Northern France and Siegfried Line Campaigns
author: Wainstein, Leonard
organization: Institute for Defense Analyses, 400 Army-Navy Drive, Arlington, VA 22202
data_description:
a. The SIEGFRIE data are taken from Table 5 (page 17) of the source. The source obtained its information from official US Army histories and available archival records such as Daily Summaries, SITREPS, G1 Journals, etc.

b. (p v, Preface) "The research presented in this paper is in the area of historical combat statistics for possible use as input to simulation models. ... The purpose of this paper is *not* to attempt to establish precise relationships among the factors of rate of advance, casualties, resistance, and terrain. There is usually insufficient numerical data for that even on a one-sided basis. Rather it is hoped that some general relationships--some proportions--will emerge that will be of use to model-builders."

c. The data consist of a representative sample of 40 attacks in which an advance of at least 300 yards was gained by allied infantry divisions in NW Europe during WWII. Of these, 35 are from the American attack on the Siegfried Line between 11 September and 16 December 1944, and 5 are from the final US counterattack phase of the Ardennes campaign (January of 1945). An indication of the terrain, degree of resistance, Allied strength, and battle casualties is included.

d. (p 1) "It should be stressed that many attacks fail to gain any ground, and these 90 advances were chosen because they did show an advance. Later, the approximate percent of all attacks in which advances occurred is determined." (p 15) "... I have arbitrarily considered that advances of under 300 yards represented no advance."

e. Distance is not defined, but presumably is FEBA displacement.

f. The time interval is defined as (p 10) "For simplicity's sake, a single day has been established as the base unit, despite the fact that in nearly every case the action lasted less than a full day and, for most actions, even less than the daylight period of the day. The purpose of the study is not to determine rates of advance on an hourly basis, but rather to determine the scale of the forward movement achieved in a good-sized sample."

g. (p 1) "Only bald statistics are presented, since, for purposes of statistical analysis and simulation, descriptive text on each battle really contributes little beyond some additional understanding of factors that cannot be quantified."

h. (p 5) "Terrain has been categorized as (1) open, (2) mixed, and (3) close or difficult. The word *mixed* thus includes the two commonly used descriptors, *moderately open* and *moderately close*, the distinction between which is really rather fine and essentially judgmental." (p 8) "... it is generally not possible to distinguish what proportion of an action occurred in a town versus the proportion that occurred on the open ground around it."

i. (pp 8-9, *passim*) "In the absence of German strength figures comparable to those obtainable for US units, degree of resistance rather than force ratio or enemy posture has been used as the descriptor for the enemy. ... The degree of enemy entrenchment--fortified position, prepared position, etc.--is not the best descriptor, since it is the fighting spirit of resistance maintained by the troops, as much as the strength of their position, that ultimately determines degree of resistance. ... In the Normandy cases, three simple categories of resistance are used: heavy, moderate, and light. For the Siegfried Line cases, five categories are used because the records employed a further breakdown of descriptor: heavy, moderate to heavy, moderate, light to moderate, and light. ... The descriptor terms are those generally used in reference to the actions in the official histories. Yet in several cases the term used does not appear to accord with the casualties suffered. ... It is obvious that no standard measure exists for the relationship between degree of resistance and casualties ..."

j. (p 10) "While the actions listed all involved a single division, it should be understood that the entire division was not always involved. Attacks involving two or three regiments were most common, while single regiment attacks are also included, since they did represent an effort mounted by a division in which the division artillery and tank units invariably participated. There are also included cases where all three regiments or brigades attacked simultaneously, but divisional attacks using only a portion of the division were the norm. Battle really was a contest between regimental-sized units with their supporting elements."

k. (p 15) Based on "a hasty search," for the Normandy-Northern France area, 40 out of 371 division attack days showed "no" advance (i.e, advances of less than 300 yards). (p 20) For the Siegfried Line area, 17 out of 137 division attack days showed "no" advance.

l. (p 21) "The variations (in Tables 4 and 8) relating terrain type to degree of resistance are so marked that any average [relating rate of advance to degree of resistance] is highly questionable." Apparently Wainstein is here referring to the marked tendency for "heavy" resistance and "close" terrain to occur together. The combined cross-tabulation for all the data in this report is as follows, where we have collapsed the Siegfried Line resistance categories to three:

| Terrain Class | Heavy | Moderate | Light | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open | 4 | 0 | 9 | 13 |
| Mixed | 13 | 17 | 14 | 44 |
| Close | 22 | 8 | 3 | 33 |
| Total | 39 | 25 | 26 | 90 |
discussion_and_comments:
a. The source table gives advances as "Actual or Daily Average of Advance." These we first converted into total distance advanced by multiplying by the duration of the action in days, and then into an average rate of advance per day by dividing by the number of days. The author's accompanying discussion of the quality of the data is sound and suggests the care with which these data were assembled. However, in statistical terms they are a "convenience sample," and not necessarily a random one.

b. The limitation to advances of 300 yards or more is arbitrary and unfortunate. Also, it would have been better had the source given at least a general description of the portion of the division actually participating in the attacks.

c. The association between degree of resistance and terrain reinforces the suspicion that there is a pervasive systematic connection here--possibly due to the defender's tendency whenever possible to select "close/difficult" terrain for his most determined stands. An alternative is to postulate that attackers tend to perceive the resistance as heavy when the terrain is "close," i.e., that the association is caused by the vicious circle alluded to elsewhere. However, the latter postulate does imply a lack of professional objectivity in the attacker's perception of the situation that we are loathe to presume without good cause, although it is well-known that even professionals can be victimized by such misperceptions from time to time.

d. In some cases, the original data table's dates spanned by the action are inconsistent with its durations in days. In such cases, we assumed that the dates were accurate and adjusted the durations accordingly. Note that some of the strength values in the original table were estimated, and that in one case the battle casualties are not for the same period as for the advance.
data_table_notes: These advances are presumably by forces that were heavily engaged.

title: Major Front Movements and the Role of Armored Forces
author: Wainstein, Leonard
organization: Institute for Defense Analyses, 400 Army-Navy Drive, Arlington, VA 22202
data_description:
a. The WAINSTEI data are taken from Tables II-1, II-4, II-5, II-6, II-7, II-8, II-9, II-10, II-11, II-12, II-13, II-15, IV-2, and IV-3 of the source. The source obtained its information from a variety of documents, but for the most part unit histories and other official and quasi-official histories, supplemented by books, articles and reports by reputable military historians.

b. (p S-1, Summary) "This study examines major campaigns from 1939 to 1973 in order to determine how fast armies have moved and specifically the armored components of them. It has also tried to illustrate some of the factors that influence the advance of armored formations." (p I-1, Introduction) "An examination was undertaken of the Second World War, Korea, Vietnam, the Indo-Pakistan clashes of 1965 and 1971, and the Arab-Israeli wars of 1956, 1967, and 1973 in order to determine what lessons in these armored operations could provide insights for the future."

c. Distance is defined as the maximum front movement. (p II-1) "Nevertheless, it should be stressed that measurement of map distances with dividers is obviously a form of macro-measurement. There can be no claim to precision but, on the other hand, the distances are reasonably accurate. Because the even 'smoothed' FEBA exists only in the model builder's imagination, it often becomes difficult to decide the point of maximum forward movement. Some degree of judgment by the analyst has therefore been necessary." (p II-18) "It is often unclear, too, how much of a force has reached the utmost point of penetration. 'Elements of ... ' is the expression commonly found and this could have been a tiny reconnaissance unit."

d. Situational descriptors are defined as follows: (p II-1) "Each campaign is described in terms of date, duration, maximum front movement, and average miles per day from start point to the point of maximum penetration. The phasing of individual campaigns is also to some degree artificial, but the source texts present them in this fashion." Occasional (but rather general) remarks about the nature of the terrain, bottlenecks, degree of opposition, etc. are provided in the accompanying discussion.
discussion_and_comments:
a. The source data are voluminous and include information apparently not available elsewhere. However, they contain a large number of obvious typographical errors. Also, the time intervals very often are in error. To the extent that we were able to recognize such errors, we corrected them, but it is possible that not all were found.

b. The source gives two separate tables for Eastern Front campaigns. The source's Table II-11 is based on *The West Point Atlas of American Wars*, and its Table II-12 is based on Ziemke's book. This is because (p II-24) "[With regard to information in *The West Point Atlas of American Wars* and in Ziemke, Earl F., *Army Historical Series*, 'Stalingrad to Berlin: The German Defeat in the East,' Office of Chief of Military History, Dept. of the Army, Washington, DC, 1968] Where they overlap in time ... the data are noticeably different. However, both are reliable sources and no attempt at reconciliation of the data will be attempted." We have not attempted to resolve the differences either, but have given both in our data base. Users are cautioned not to double-count these actions.

c. The source, on pp II-30 to II-34, provides a very informative discussion of the Soviet WWII Manchurian campaign. In particular it points out that the Japanese forces were "little more than a hollow shell," outnumbered by 416,000 to 72,000 in terms of troops in combat units, with half the authorized number of machineguns and no antitank weapons, and short of artillery and ammunition. The whole campaign was conducted after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August). "The Sixth Guards Tank Army met no resistance at all for the first four days [9-13 August 1945] and virtually none in the whole campaign. The two mechanized corps [accompanying it] used extended march order, each in six to eight parallel columns. ... Japanese forces had begun to surrender on 15 August in response to the Emperor's declaration of the war's end. The Soviets for obvious political purposes refused to accept the 15 August surrender, thereby continuing their advance to reach their set territorial objectives, ... They accepted only the 2 September surrender in Tokyo harbor." The analysis of rates of advance in the Soviet Manchurian campaign should take into consideration its special circumstances.

d. The source's Table III-1 and Table III-2 were taken from and duplicate information available in Andrews' paper (see our data base ANDREWS). The source's Tables V-1 and V-2 were taken from the ORALFORE report and add nothing to our data base ORALFORE.

e. The source's Figure II-1 gives information from the US Strategic Bombing Survey (Vol 64A, "The Impact of the Allied War Effort on German Logistics") for "Representative German Divisonal Moves to Cherbourg Peninsula" in response to the Allied landings. These data are given in tabular form below. In each case, the first segment of the move was by rail and the last by road.

title: The Persian Expedition (Anabasis)
author: Xenophon
organization: Penguin Books, New York, NY
data_description:
a. The Xenophon data were compiled from the source by Dr. Robert L. Helmbold of CAA. They consist of the 38 instances in which Xenophon mentions in his narrative both a distance and a corresponding duration of advance.

b. The data are for episodes that occurred during the advance and retreat of about 10,000 Greek mercenaries through the Persian Empire in 401-400 BC. During their advance, the Greek mercenaries were part of Cyrus the Younger's rebel army, but when he was killed during the battle of Cunaxa the Greeks were isolated deep within the hostile Persian empire. For the first month of their retreat from Cunaxa, the Greeks were escorted peaceably by Persian forces. Thereafter they were severely harried by the Persians and by semicivilized mountain tribes until they reached the safety of the Greek colonies along the southern shore of the Black Sea. Throughout, the Greeks moved entirely by foot, supported by pack animals. Only a handful of their highest-ranking commanders had horses.
discussion_and_comments:
a. The translator of the source states in his introduction that "I have attempted to use as many English words as possible; consequently I have, for example, got rid of the 'parasang,' so familiar to beginners in Greek, and turned it, rather inaccurately, into miles. The fact is that the distance represented by a parasang differs in accordance with the nature of the country over which one is marching, so it is impossible to give an exact measurement that would not be insupportably cumbrous for each day's march." Based on some preliminary analysis of the data, the translator probably has rounded off the mile values and may have favored values that correspond to 15 miles/day.

b. For the most part, it is not clear just what type of terrain or weather obtained for Xenophon's advances, or the extent to which enemy forces opposed them. Where it is clear, it is so indicated in the XENOPHON data base.
data_table_notes: These advances were by forces that were lightly engaged.
